asio is Boost.Asio natively, and in the browser Boost.Asio’s own io_context suspended into the page’s event loop, in C++20, one of the libraries of webcpp. A program written against Boost.Asio, main() and io_context::run() included, runs unchanged in a browser: compiled with Emscripten, asio adds only what Boost lacks there, the configuration Asio needs to build, what wakes run from a browser event, and a limit on the handlers one turn runs, so that the page keeps rendering.

WASIp2 provides single-threaded timers, TCP/UDP, pollable-driven forward DNS, supplied CLI streams, Cobalt and optional source-built TLS. See Build for WASIp2 for its explicit limitations. WASIp3 provides timers, TCP/UDP, waitable-driven forward DNS, Cobalt and the same optional TLS provider, with single-thread and experimental cooperative-thread profiles. See Target and variant capabilities for their limits and the features available in each target variant.

Find your way through the guide

The guide follows Diataxis: choose a path for what you need now. All paths share the compiled examples and generated API reference on this page.

  • Learn by doing: start with Tutorial: your first asynchronous program.

  • Complete a task: build and load a program, configure a turn limit, schedule and cancel timers, link a Cobalt program, build for WASIp3, or test your application.

  • Understand the design: read Why asio, A turn at a time, Browser events and Runtime allocations.

  • Look up a contract: use Target and variant capabilities, The names, Guarantees and the generated API reference.

Tutorial: your first asynchronous program

We will run a program that prints a message, waits for a timer and returns from its event loop. You will see when a scheduled handler actually runs and why the context stays alive while a timer wait is pending.

You need basic C++ knowledge, a webcpp checkout, b2 and a configured native C++20 compiler. For the second run, you also need the Emscripten and Node setup described in Building. Run the commands below from the superproject root. No web server is needed for this first exercise.

1. Open the program

Open libs/asio/example/asio_quick_start.cpp. This is the complete program we will compile, including its headers:

#include <webcpp/asio/io_context.hpp>
#include <webcpp/asio/steady_timer.hpp>

#include <webcpp/test/exit_status.hpp>

#include <boost/asio/post.hpp>

#include <chrono>
#include <cstdio>

namespace asio = webcpp::asio;
using namespace std::chrono_literals;

int main() {
    asio::io_context io;
    asio::steady_timer timer(io);

    boost::asio::post(io, [&timer] {
        std::puts("posted");
        timer.expires_after(50ms);
        timer.async_wait([](boost::system::error_code ec) {
            if (ec) {
                std::printf("timer error: %d\n", ec.value());
            } else {
                std::puts("timer fired");
            }
        });
    });

    const auto handlers = io.run();  // lint-run: main owns the program's event loop
    std::printf("run returned %zu handlers\n", handlers);
    return webcpp::test::exit_status(0);
}

The context owns the event loop. The timer belongs to that context and stays alive until main ends. post schedules the first handler; it does not call it immediately. That handler prints posted, arms the timer and registers its completion handler. This sequence keeps the output order the same even if the machine pauses before entering run.

2. Run it natively

b2 libs/asio/example//asio_quick_start.output

The build compiles and executes the program, then compares its output with the file beside it, asio_quick_start.expected. On success, b2 saves the captured output in asio_quick_start.output at the build path printed by its run-and-compare action. Open that file; its contents should be:

posted
timer fired
run returned 2 handlers

The last line uses webcpp’s example-test helper to report completion, including after an Asyncify suspension. It leaves page modules without the Node harness unchanged.

Notice that run returns after both handlers have run. The timer’s 50 ms is a requested delay, not a promise about exact wall-clock execution time. The output deliberately shows no measured duration.

3. Run the same source as WebAssembly

b2 toolset=emscripten libs/asio/example//asio_quick_start.output

Node executes the generated WebAssembly using JSPI. Its .output file contains exactly the same three lines. Next, run it with Asyncify:

b2 toolset=emscripten webcpp-suspend=asyncify libs/asio/example//asio_quick_start.output

Again the output is unchanged. These runs exercise the source and its suspension under Node; loading a page in a browser is a separate step in Loading the variant a browser runs. If b2 cannot find a compiler or Node, check Building before changing the program. If the output differs, the example runner prints the difference and fails the build.

4. Follow the next piece of work

You have now run the same event loop natively and with both WebAssembly suspension variants. Follow How to schedule deadlines and cancel a wait to schedule several deadlines and cancel a wait, or How to configure the turn limit to configure a finite chain of posted work. For the reason the browser needs a turn limit, read A turn at a time. Exact contracts are in Guarantees and the generated API reference.

Why asio

Boost.Asio is the ground of asynchronous C++: Boost.Beast, Boost.Cobalt, Boost.MySQL, Boost.Redis and many others are written on it, as templates over its executors, its completion tokens and its stream concepts. asio keeps all of that and changes one thing, where the waiting happens. Natively it is Boost.Asio itself. Compiled with Emscripten it is still Boost.Asio’s own io_context, whose run suspends into the browser’s event loop, so that two worlds meet.

C++'s asynchronous libraries reach the browser. What is written on Asio’s model runs in a page with the same code, because the io_context, the executors and the timers are Boost’s own. Boost.Cobalt runs on asio’s io_context and executors unchanged, its timers included, since Cobalt’s io::steady_timer wraps Asio’s; its co_main runs unchanged too, and asio gives it the turn limit by replacing the one function of Cobalt’s that runs the io_context. Boost.Beast is templates over stream concepts, AsyncReadStream and AsyncWriteStream: its messages, parsers, serializers and buffers compile and run in the browser as they are, and its timeouts are Boost timers, which fire there. Its HTTP and WebSocket algorithms run unchanged over a byte stream a program names as their next layer: a socket of asio’s whose transport a later library provides, or a WebRTC channel’s. Beast’s own tcp_stream wraps Boost’s socket, never asio’s, and over plain TCP nothing runs, since a browser gives no raw sockets; there webcpp’s beast library gives Beast’s interfaces over the browser’s own WebSocket and fetch. Any other library written on Asio’s model, its completion tokens and its executors, follows.

The browser’s asynchronous model reaches C++. The web’s APIs are asynchronous: promises, events, streams. asio makes a promise and an event source Asio operations: a JavaScript promise is awaitable with any completion token, co_await, a callback or a Cobalt task, and an event source is an operation that completes on the event, so that C++ writes the web’s programs in the web’s own model, and in C++'s.

Emscripten 6.0.11 already makes Boost.Asio’s io_context::run suspend into the browser. What asio adds there, the threads configuration on Emscripten, the turn limit and the wake from browser events, is proven here first, to be offered to Boost.Asio upstream later.

The names

asio’s targets are native, emscripten, wasip2 and wasip3. The table below compares native and browser interfaces; Target and variant capabilities specifies the WASIp2 and WASIp3 subsets, which keep Boost’s socket and timer types. A name of asio is Boost.Asio’s own, or a type with Boost.Asio’s interface where the browser needs one of its own:

Name Native Emscripten

webcpp::asio::io_context

A class derived from boost::asio::io_context; its run family is Boost’s.

The same class: Boost’s scheduler and reactor, the reactor made at construction, and the run family composed with the limit on the handlers one turn runs.

Executors, post, dispatch, bind_executor, completion tokens, co_spawn, Boost.Cobalt

Boost.Asio’s.

Boost.Asio’s, unchanged.

webcpp::asio::steady_timer, system_timer, basic_waitable_timer

Aliases of Boost’s.

Aliases of Boost’s, in the reactor’s timer queue, which run waits on.

Promises and events as operations

None: nothing of the browser exists.

A JavaScript promise and an event source, each an Asio operation.

WebSocket and HTTP clients

Boost.Beast.

webcpp’s beast library: Beast’s interfaces over the browser’s WebSocket and fetch.

ip::tcp, ip::udp: sockets, acceptor, resolver

Aliases of Boost’s.

Class templates of asio’s with Boost’s interfaces: each operation of a socket or an acceptor completes with operation_not_supported unless a transport provides it, and the resolver completes with the entries the browser streams of webcpp’s beast library accept.

ssl: context, stream_base, verify_*, host_name_verification

Aliases of Boost’s, in <webcpp/asio/ssl.hpp>, which brings OpenSSL natively, so that <webcpp/asio.hpp> leaves it out.

A record of the program’s TLS settings, which only the browser streams of webcpp’s beast library read.

A program includes <webcpp/asio.hpp> and writes webcpp::asio:: where it would write boost::asio:: for the types above; every other name of Boost.Asio, post, co_spawn, use_awaitable, bind_executor and the rest, it keeps naming directly. The io_context is a class of its own on both targets, so that a program sets its options the same way everywhere; its executor is boost::asio::io_context::executor_type and it converts to boost::asio::io_context&, so code written against either interoperates. Every other name is an alias of Boost’s natively.

The io_context takes its options, io_context_options, as the last argument of each of Boost’s constructors: with none, with an allocator, which it allocates its services and its objects’ state with, and with Boost’s hint of the concurrency it will see, with or without an allocator, so that Boost’s idiom io_context io{1} compiles unchanged. Its one option, max_handlers_per_turn, 100 by default, bounds the handlers one turn of its run family runs on emscripten before it yields to the browser; 0 is taken as 1. Natively and on WASIp2/P3 the options are accepted and change nothing, since no browser page waits on these loops.

On emscripten, /webcpp/asio//asio also gives every program the configuration Asio needs to build there, and the link flags of its suspension variant (Building).

Target and variant capabilities

This reference covers the public feature families of webcpp::asio and its Cobalt build target. It does not promise every feature of the complete Boost installation. Supported means the implementation provides the feature; limited requires the qualification below; unverified is not a portability promise. Native behavior also depends on the operating system.

For the explicit feature-by-feature intersection of threads and exception handling, use Feature matrix by library and build profile. It separates Asio from Cobalt and distinguishes public support, isolated probes and unverified combinations.

variant=debug and variant=release select build optimization, not different APIs. The new WASIp3 runtime verification uses Release builds. JSPI and Asyncify are browser suspension variants; they are not WASIp3 variants. The WASIp3 thread setting and exception setting are independent choices, subject to the SDK runtime availability above. Cooperative threads suspend at blocking WASI operations; this does not provide simultaneous CPU execution on multiple cores.

Feature matrix by library and build profile

This records the WebCPP integration and capability-completion work verified on 2026-11-03, using Boost 1.92.0, Emscripten 6.0.11 and wasi-sdk 34.0. The project now selects Wasmtime 50.0.1 for its regression suites; the original isolated probes used Wasmtime 49.0.3. It is not a list of everything those upstream projects might support in other builds. The Asio target is /webcpp/asio//asio; the Cobalt integration is /webcpp/asio//cobalt, using Boost.Cobalt’s names. Do not infer that an Asio feature has also been tested through a Cobalt wrapper or completion token.

Each cell describes the named feature, not every overload or possible input. Read the profile availability table first: an unavailable profile makes all of its public features unavailable, even if an isolated source file compiles.

Unavailable through this integration or the tested toolchain.

Build integration blocked: WebCPP rejects the library target before compilation. Read the named blocker; this does not establish a platform limit.

P

C

Compile only: an isolated source compiles; linking and execution are unverified.

N/A

The feature is specific to another environment.

Native S is not a promise of no threads. The native build does not set BOOST_ASIO_DISABLE_THREADS. Boost may use internal threads, for example for asynchronous name resolution. Explicitly disabling Asio threads is a different configuration and must be applied consistently to the application and compiled dependencies. It does not disable unrelated libraries’ threads.

Browser S sets BOOST_ASIO_DISABLE_THREADS; explicit M enables pthreads in the application and compiled dependencies. WASIp3 S also disables Asio threads. WASIp3 M uses cooperative threads, not simultaneous CPU execution on multiple cores. The missing cooperative EH runtime is a limitation of the SDK distribution tested here, not proof that threads and exceptions are fundamentally incompatible.

variant=release/debug changes optimization, not these feature declarations. The WASIp3 evidence here uses Release. Native operating-system features remain subject to Boost and the host OS; macOS results are not Windows or Linux tests.

L for sockets means that the default transport reports operation_not_supported; the application supplies a transport with the required semantics. This is not raw browser TCP/UDP access. Browser HTTPS or WSS capabilities do not by themselves supply an Asio/OpenSSL stream adapter. The SSL settings record does not encrypt data. See Sockets and transports.

The run family must execute on a stack configured for suspension. A browser yield gives the host an opportunity to run; it does not guarantee a timer deadline or a rendered frame. EH on uses Wasm exceptions with JSPI and the configured JavaScript exception mechanism with Asyncify.

Both profiles use native asynchronous forward lookup with a waitable-backed reactor descriptor. Deferred initiation, real localhost lookup, timer progress, cancellation and allocator routing are tested. The cooperative lane also checks two-runner cancellation after the host waitable joins the active wait set. External DNS and network access still depend on host capabilities.

UDP gather/scatter preserves one datagram and uses the caller-associated allocator, including connected sends, truncation, empty buffers and cancellation. The separate context/timer/post counters now cover all three supported WASIp3 profiles; narrowly attributed libc wakeup-pipe allocations remain outside the Asio allocator contract. These scenarios are not a complete audit of every operation. Socket-option limits are in WASIp3 limits and error behavior. TLS support does not automatically validate a Cobalt TLS completion token or boost::cobalt::io::ssl::stream.

Numeric asynchronous resolution is tested through Cobalt’s compiled resolver in the supported profiles above. How the Cobalt source integration works

The target builds the normal compiled archive, replacing its endpoint and acceptor source files with checked private copies. The private header overlay uses Asio capability macros to omit unsupported local-socket, signal and serial APIs. Seqpacket declarations are omitted when that socket type is unavailable. Single-thread builds omit the thread source and declaration; cooperative builds include it. Native and browser builds retain their original sources and headers.

The application, archive and replacement runner use the same patched Asio headers, thread profile and exception setting. No system Cobalt archive is linked, and installed Boost files are never modified. Input/output hashes pin the compatibility patch to Boost 1.92. A changed upstream input is rejected.

The public-target tests cover both Cobalt completion tokens applied to Asio sockets and Cobalt’s own compiled TCP/UDP wrappers, with IPv4 loopback traffic, refused TCP connections, TCP EOF and TCP/UDP cancellation. TLS tests add the ordinary Asio/OpenSSL stream and Cobalt token, with custom or embedded CAs and peer identity verification.

SDK 34.0 maps nonzero command returns to failure: the host statuses are 0 for co_return 0 and 1 for co_return 7. The status driver checks both output and status, so a trap cannot satisfy the failure case. No host shutdown protocol has been added. See Why the runner changes and Completion and limitations.

Require a capability at compile time

<webcpp/asio/config.hpp> defines the following read-only macros as 0 or 1. Use #if, not #ifdef, to inspect them. Do not define these capabilities on the command line: the header rejects attempts to override them.

Macro suffix after WEBCPP_ASIO_ Meaning of 1

HAS_SOCKET_BACKEND

Native/WASI TCP and UDP backend, subject to runtime grants and options.

HAS_OPENSSL_BACKEND

This target supports the optional source-built OpenSSL provider.

HAS_HOST_DNS

Forward lookup through the native/WASI host, subject to host DNS policy.

HAS_REVERSE_DNS

Native reverse lookup; the WASI interface is forward-only.

HAS_THREADS

Boost.Asio thread support is enabled in this build, including cooperative threads.

HAS_BROWSER_BRIDGE

Emscripten JavaScript events and Promises can reach the executor.

HAS_BROWSER_WORKERS

Emscripten pthread build with Asio thread support.

HAS_WASI_STDIO

The WASIp2 pollable CLI stream adapter is available.

HAS_LOCAL_SOCKETS, HAS_SIGNALS, HAS_SERIAL_PORT

Native target with the corresponding Boost.Asio facility enabled.

WEBCPP_ASIO_HAS_OPENSSL=1 is different: it declares that the optional compiled dependency was selected. /webcpp/asio//openssl and //tls supply it together with the matching provider. Outside B2, the application must also supply the matching OpenSSL headers and libraries. Merely defining it cannot satisfy the linker. ssl.hpp rejects native/WASI use without that dependency; Emscripten keeps its portable TLS settings record.

Define a WEBCPP_ASIO_REQUIRE_* switch to a nonzero integer before the first WebCPP include, or on the compiler command line, to require SOCKET_BACKEND, OPENSSL, THREADS, LOCAL_SOCKETS, SIGNALS, SERIAL_PORT or REVERSE_DNS. An absent switch or a value of zero imposes no requirement. The default permits portable applications to select runtime alternatives, including browser transports. Apply configuration consistently to every translation unit.

This compiled example requires a real socket backend and still handles a runtime refusal from the host:

// State requirements before the first WebCPP include, or use a compiler define.
#define WEBCPP_ASIO_REQUIRE_SOCKET_BACKEND 1
#include <cstdio>
#include <webcpp/asio/io_context.hpp>
#include <webcpp/asio/ip/tcp.hpp>
#include <webcpp/test/exit_status.hpp>

int main() {
    webcpp::asio::io_context context;
    webcpp::asio::ip::tcp::socket socket(context);
    boost::system::error_code error;
    if (socket.open(webcpp::asio::ip::tcp::v4(), error)) {
        // A compiled backend does not imply that the host granted socket access.
        const auto message = error.message();
        (void)std::fprintf(stderr, "socket open: %s\n", message.c_str());
        return webcpp::test::exit_status(1);
    }
    std::puts("TCP socket opened");
    return webcpp::test::exit_status(0);
}
TCP socket opened

The browser-specific headers diagnose a non-Emscripten target before including Emscripten headers. wasi/stdio_stream.hpp diagnoses targets without the P2 CLI adapter. B2 rejects unsupported SDK/thread/EH combinations and checks the private WASI descriptor ABI. A compiler cannot determine network grants, available peers, trust roots, a page’s isolation headers or whether a host import will block. Those conditions retain runtime errors or the documented host behavior.
