OpenSSL local coverage includes native macOS arm64 single/multi with exceptions on/off using Clang, WASIp2 and WASIp3 single with exceptions on/off, and WASIp3 cooperative with exceptions off. A GCC 15 native multi-threaded build with exceptions also passed the TLS tests. Linux Clang/GCC mappings are implemented but not runtime-tested on this macOS host. The native MSVC recipe is implemented; this local macOS matrix does not establish Windows runtime coverage. The source library uses OS threads natively and cooperative threads on WASIp3; it does not make cooperative execution CPU-parallel. TLS tests cover verified handshakes, asynchronous application data, clean shutdown and rejected peer identities. The embedded CA factory’s trust policy, update procedure and local checks are documented in How-to: configure trusted certificate authorities.

The browser’s default socket transport reports operation_not_supported for network operations. The browser resolver does not perform DNS; see Sockets and transports. A TLS settings record is not a TLS implementation.

WASIp3 limits and error behavior

  • TCP buffer sequences advance one nonempty buffer per syscall when necessary. Partial reads and writes are valid Asio behavior; composed async_read and async_write continue until their completion condition is met. No temporary heap buffer is introduced to concatenate a sequence.

  • UDP send_to and async_send_to concatenate multiple nonempty buffers into one datagram because the tested wasi-libc does not provide sendmsg. Concatenation visits the entire sequence before Asio’s native iovec limit. It copies the payload once into temporary storage: the context allocator supplies synchronous storage, and the handler’s associated allocator supplies asynchronous storage. The operation owns asynchronous storage until completion or destruction and releases it before invoking the handler. Scalar, empty and single-nonempty-buffer sends need no temporary allocation or payload copy. The gather path rejects payloads above 65,535 bytes with message_size before allocating or reading their data; the host may enforce a smaller IP limit. Allocation failure follows the supplied allocator’s failure behavior.

  • Connected send / async_send use the same single-datagram gather path. Multi-buffer receives read one datagram into temporary storage and scatter the received bytes across the destination sequence. A short destination truncates the datagram; its remainder is not delivered as another packet. Empty buffers do not split a datagram. Empty datagrams are delivered. Scratch allocation follows the synchronous context or asynchronous handler allocator, as for sends.

  • Synchronous resolution uses wasi-libc. Actual hostname lookup requires host permission; numeric resolution does not need DNS. Both thread profiles use the native asynchronous forward-lookup import and a waitable-backed descriptor for async_resolve. Initiation is deferred through the executor and other timers progress while the lookup is pending. Resolver-wide and per-operation cancellation preserve the normal completion channel. No hidden thread or periodic DNS polling is introduced. Canonical names, mapped-address policies and asynchronous reverse lookup are explicitly unsupported.

  • Interface-name scopes such as %eth0 are rejected. Decimal IPv6 scopes in the range 0 through 4294967295 are accepted.

  • Missing socket options, including linger, broadcast, debug, don’t-route, out-of-band-inline and low-water marks, report operation_not_supported. Other options remain subject to wasi-libc and host support. Multicast and detailed socket-option interoperability have not been validated.

  • WASI has no ESHUTDOWN. The port maps Asio’s shut_down to EPIPE, which wasi-libc uses; it therefore shares the numeric value of broken_pipe.

  • Error-code overloads and asynchronous completion retain their error channels. With exceptions disabled, invoking a throwing overload on an error can still reach Boost’s fatal exception handler. Prefer explicit error-code/result paths.

  • Cobalt uses the same platform restrictions through its public B2 target. Its async resolver uses the same native lookup in both thread profiles. TLS through Asio/OpenSSL with Cobalt tokens uses application-selected trust roots and host network capabilities; embedded roots require no certificate filesystem preopen. See TLS: build OpenSSL from source on native and WASI and How-to: configure trusted certificate authorities.

These are current port boundaries, not claims that WASIp3 itself can never support the missing operations. The compatibility patch belongs to Boost.Asio’s platform layer; implementing the missing POSIX entry points such as sendmsg/recvmsg belongs in wasi-libc. The current port avoids pretending those entry points or process signals exist.

Building

asio is developed inside the webcpp superproject, as a Boost library is developed inside Boost. Its headers share Boost’s executor model; the browser bridge and optional Cobalt entry point have compiled support units. A b2 program uses /webcpp/asio//asio on native, Emscripten and WASIp2/P3:

exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/asio//asio ;

The target adds asio’s headers, Boost’s and the webcpp configuration dependency. <webcpp/asio/config.hpp> includes <webcpp/config.hpp> first; WEBCPP_NO_EXCEPTIONS disables asio’s throwing APIs even when the compiler supports exceptions. An explicit WEBCPP_ASIO_NO_EXCEPTIONS remains supported. On emscripten the target also supplies everything else a program needs there: the define Asio needs to build, embind, the JavaScript functions asio calls, compiled once in src/browser_src.cpp, the link flags of the program’s suspension variant, and the variant in the program’s name:

alias asio : : : : <include>include <library>/boost//headers
  <library>/webcpp/config//config
  <target-os>windows:<library>/webcpp/asio-windows//headers
  <toolset>clang-wasip2:<library>/webcpp/asio-wasip2//headers
  <toolset>clang-wasip2:<source>/webcpp/asio-wasip2//pollable
  <toolset>clang-wasip3:<library>/webcpp/asio-wasip3//headers
  <toolset>emscripten,<threading>single:<define>BOOST_ASIO_DISABLE_THREADS
  <toolset>emscripten:<linkflags>-lembind
  <toolset>emscripten:<linkflags>-Wl,--export=emscripten_stack_get_current
  <toolset>emscripten:<linkflags>-Wl,--export=_emscripten_stack_restore
  <toolset>emscripten,<threading>multi:<linkflags>-Wl,--wrap=__syscall_poll
  <toolset>emscripten:<source>browser-src
  <toolset>emscripten,<webcpp-suspend>jspi:<linkflags>-sJSPI
  <toolset>emscripten,<webcpp-suspend>asyncify:<linkflags>-sASYNCIFY
  <conditional>@asyncify-stack
  <toolset>emscripten:<tag>@webcpp%suspend-tag ;

The Emscripten S profile sets BOOST_ASIO_DISABLE_THREADS. Explicit threading=multi enables pthreads consistently in the application, browser support unit and optional Cobalt archive. Asio’s inline namespace differs with and without threads, so all translation units and compiled dependencies must use matching settings.

The bridge’s JavaScript uses stackSave and stackRestore. On Emscripten 6.0.11, their native dependencies must survive the native link before EM_JS_DEPS is processed. The target therefore exports emscripten_stack_get_current and _emscripten_stack_restore explicitly, including in optimized JSPI builds. A build outside b2 must keep the same link flags shown above.

Browser workers and main-thread callbacks

Select threading=multi together with either suspension variant and exception setting. The public target supplies -pthread through the toolset and the threaded main-poll adapter. It does not move main to a worker automatically. The M-only -Wl,--wrap=__syscall_poll adapter uses the pinned SDK’s async poll on the actual browser main thread; worker waits retain the SDK proxy route. This private SDK boundary must be rechecked when Emscripten is upgraded.

A browser io_context must run on the thread that constructed it. Other threads may post ordinary C++ work to its executor. One context does not support simultaneous runners; keep separate contexts per worker. Running it from a different thread triggers a checked-build assertion and returns zero when assertions are disabled, before accessing thread-local JavaScript values.

browser::main_thread_context supplies an Asio executor for DOM callbacks. Construct and destroy that context on the actual browser main thread; copy its executor to workers and use boost::asio::post or bind_executor. Obtain JavaScript objects inside the main callback and send ordinary C++ data back to the worker. Do not move emscripten::val handles between threads. The context must outlive calls using its executors, and destruction must not overlap such calls. If a callback destroys its context, an external allocator resource must outlive the callback because queue control survives until it returns. Queued handlers are discarded during shutdown. Handler storage follows its associated allocator; the SDK owns its separate queue/notification storage.

A main-executor callback runs on an ordinary browser callback stack. It must not call a JSPI/Asyncify suspending import or drive the context’s run family. Normal C++ coroutine suspension that returns to its caller is a different mechanism. If moving or invoking a handler throws, queued handlers are discarded and further queued submissions are discarded. Inline main-thread dispatch retains its ordinary direct-call behavior. The exception propagates to the browser callback boundary; recovery after that failure is not promised. Cancellation still belongs to the originating operation; posting a callable does not add a new cancellation protocol.

The host needs a secure context, workers and shared memory. Serve the page with Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp, and check crossOriginIsolated. These deployment requirements cannot be diagnosed in config.hpp. Applications choose their worker-pool size and must retain the runtime while work is pending. Never block the browser main thread waiting for a live worker.

The local lane covers JSPI/Asyncify with EH on/off in an isolated Chrome page:

b2 libs/asio/test/browser//browser-workers toolset=emscripten \
  threading=multi webcpp-suspend=jspi exception-handling=on

Repeat with webcpp-suspend=asyncify and exception-handling=off for the other profiles. The driver tests actual main/worker wakeup, DOM handoff, cancellation, allocator routing, queued shutdown and Cobalt thread completion. The exact coverage appears in Browser pthread profiles.

Pinned Asyncify pthread return-value limit

A dependency-only witness is versioned in test/browser/probes/pthread_return.cpp. It suspends a pthread entry, returns pointer value 42, and joins without blocking the browser main thread. With Emscripten 6.0.11, JSPI preserves 42; Asyncify returns zero and the witness fails. This does not involve Asio. Void-return worker paths with explicit C++ result storage are tested successfully in both variants. This runtime path is not identifiable from a target define, so no broad compile-time ban is imposed.

To reproduce from the superproject root using the configured SDK:

em++ libs/asio/test/browser/probes/pthread_return.cpp \
  -pthread -sPTHREAD_POOL_SIZE=1 -sJSPI -o worker_return-jspi.js
node libs/asio/test/browser/run.mjs --mode workers worker_return-jspi.js

Replace -sJSPI with -sASYNCIFY -sASYNCIFY_STACK_SIZE=8192 and change the output name for the failing control. The failure is retained as evidence of an SDK limitation, not counted as a passing application test.

The two suspension variants

On emscripten, run suspends main into the browser’s event loop in one of two ways, each a variant of the program built from the same sources:

Variant What suspends Link flags Exceptions Browsers

jspi, the default

JavaScript Promise Integration: the suspending imports, Emscripten’s __syscall_poll and asio’s yield, are wrapped in WebAssembly.Suspending, and main, on whose stack run executes, in WebAssembly.promising.

-sJSPI

WebAssembly exceptions, -fwasm-exceptions

those with JSPI

asyncify

Emscripten’s Asyncify: the compiler instruments every function that may reach a suspending import, so that the stack unwinds into the browser and is rewound when the program resumes.

-sASYNCIFY, -sASYNCIFY_STACK_SIZE, measured

JavaScript-based exceptions, -fexceptions

every browser

A build asks for a variant with the feature webcpp-suspend, on b2’s command line, b2 toolset=emscripten webcpp-suspend=asyncify, or in a program’s requirements, <webcpp-suspend>asyncify. The feature is propagated, so that every library a program uses is built for its variant, and composite, since Asyncify does not work with WebAssembly exceptions: emcc only warns, and the program traps at run time with RuntimeError: unreachable when it suspends inside a catch block. So asyncify asks for JavaScript-based exceptions itself, and jspi keeps b2’s WebAssembly ones; a build with exception-handling=off compiles with -fno-exceptions in either:

feature.feature webcpp-suspend : jspi asyncify : propagated composite ;
feature.compose <webcpp-suspend>asyncify : <exception-handling-method>js ;

Emscripten finds the suspending imports itself, so no list of them is given. ASYNCIFY_IGNORE_INDIRECT is not set, since the path from main to the reactor’s select passes a virtual call, Asio’s scheduler_task::run. Asyncify adds instrumentation and increases the program size. With -O3 and exceptions enabled, the release examples measured 1.88 to 1.91 times the JSPI WebAssembly size. The ratio depends on the optimization profile and exception setting; see How to compare release sizes and timings for the six-profile matrix with exceptions on and off, separate JavaScript byte counts, build and execution timings, and reproduction commands.

Asyncify’s stack

Asyncify saves a suspension in a stack of its own, of a fixed size, which ASYNCIFY_STACK_SIZE sets and Emscripten allocates at every suspension: each frame from main down to the suspending import writes its locals there as it unwinds, and a suspension that does not fit traps with RuntimeError: unreachable, which Emscripten follows, in a build with assertions, with "may be due to ASYNCIFY_STACK_SIZE not being large enough". The trap is certain, at every suspension that deep, but only there. So asio does not keep Emscripten’s default: it sets the size to at least twice the deepest suspension its tests reach, measured exactly, as the bytes each unwind wrote, read from Asyncify’s own data when the unwind stops. In the measurements of 2026-10-11, the deepest build was one compiled with optimization and linked without it, as b2’s release variant links on emscripten: its deepest suspension in the tests wrote 3,540 bytes, against 1,272 in a debug build. Linked with optimization, a suspension writes a sixth or less of what it writes linked without: 416 bytes at most in the tests, and 384 for the run family’s deepest path, against 2,404. Half of the stack is so left to the program’s own frames, whose depth asio cannot know.

A program that calls run deep in its code, or whose frames above run are large, measures its own suspensions the same way and asks for more with the feature asyncify-stack-size, which asio declares: in its requirements, <asyncify-stack-size>16384, or on b2’s command line, asyncify-stack-size=16384. Its values are powers of two from 8192, asio’s size and the default, to 1048576; a smaller one stops the program’s compilation at an #error of <webcpp/asio/config.hpp>, which says why. asio’s usage requirements read the feature, so that its flag ends last on emcc’s command line, where emcc keeps the last: a <linkflags> of the program’s own would come before asio’s and be ignored.

A suspension that does not fit is found when the unwind stops, after its frames wrote past Asyncify’s stack into the heap; the program aborts there. Nothing of the program runs afterwards: no destructor or atexit handler, no timer or event of asio’s; only JavaScript of the page’s own that calls an export could still enter it.

Held by asyncify_stack, with exceptions and without them, in debug, in release and in release linked with -O3, which measures every suspension of the run family, the reactor’s wait and the yield under each member that makes one, inside a try and a catch block too, and fails when one of them leaves less than half of the stack, or when the reading finds no unwind, no byte written, or no blocking poll in a reactor-wait case; by every test of the asyncify lane, which links the same size and traps if a suspension of its own does not fit; by asyncify_stack_size_default and asyncify_stack_size_raised, which read the size the program was linked with, and asyncify_stack_size_refused, which does not compile, beside asyncify_stack_size_control, which does; and by bridge_abort, in each variant, where an event called from JavaScript after the runtime aborted reaches no registration.

The reactor-wait cases keep outstanding work until a JavaScript macrotask posts the handler that releases it. Each delays entry by 25 ms, past the expiry of the former 1 ms C++ timer, and requires a poll with a nonzero timeout. A timer that already expired can finish in the initial nonblocking poll: that poll suspends too, but its shorter stack is not evidence for the waiting path. The yield cases cover run, run_for and run_until separately.

On 2026-10-14, with Emscripten 6.0.11 and Node 26.7.0, the corrected asyncify_stack test measured these maxima from scratch, in bytes:

Build Exceptions on Exceptions off

Debug

1164

844

Release, unoptimized link

2896

1940

Release, link with -O3

384

288

Each of the eleven paths with exceptions and nine without stayed below 4096 bytes, half of the configured 8192. These are measurements of the run-family test, not a bound on a user’s own call frames.

The artifacts are named and placed as Boost’s own build names and places them: one directory level per toolset, variant and property that is not the default, and a file name that carries the program’s tags joined by -, the toolset’s version, 60 for Emscripten 6.0.11, d for a debug build, and the suspension variant. The default variant adds no directory level:

Build The program app

debug, jspi

bin/emscripten-6.0.11/debug/.../app-60-d-jspi.js

debug, asyncify

bin/emscripten-6.0.11/debug/.../webcpp-suspend-asyncify/app-60-d-asyncify.js

release, jspi

bin/emscripten-6.0.11/release/.../app-60-jspi.js

each beside its .wasm.

Loading the variant a browser runs

Build a page program and its two variants with webcpp.variants:

webcpp.variants page_program : page_program.cpp : <library>/webcpp/asio//asio ;

The build writes page_program.variants.json beside the JSPI artifact. Its jspi and asyncify objects each contain a script path relative to the manifest and the WebAssembly size in bytes. Serve the manifest, both scripts and their WebAssembly files with their relative layout intact.

The loader is include/webcpp/asio/webcpp-asio-loader.mjs, shipped with the headers. A page imports its load function and calls load('page_program.variants.json'). It detects JSPI by checking whether WebAssembly.Suspending is a function, chooses jspi when it is and asyncify otherwise, and reads the artifact path from the manifest. It resolves that path relative to the final manifest URL after any HTTP redirects, imports the script and awaits its default factory. A custom fetch that supplies no response URL uses the requested manifest URL. The result is {variant, module}.

supportsJspi(scope) permits detection in a supplied scope. pick(manifest, jspi) returns {variant, script} and rejects a missing script for the selected variant. load(manifestUrl, options) accepts an explicit jspi choice, module options passed to the factory, and replacements for fetch and importModule. Failed manifest requests report their URL and HTTP status; fetch, JSON, import and initialization failures propagate to the caller. A failed JSPI load does not silently retry Asyncify.

A relative manifest URL is resolved against the page URL, or against the loader module URL where no page location exists. Factory completion is variant-dependent: the current JSPI factory awaits main, while Asyncify can resolve before a suspended main finishes. An indefinitely running JSPI program therefore reports readiness through its module callbacks; an application observes its own completion signal. The loader test waits for the program’s output, within the driver’s timeout, rather than sleeping for an assumed duration.

The browser lane loads both variants under Node using a file reader for the manifest, and in headless Chrome over loopback HTTP. It exercises this actual page program:

int main() {
    webcpp::asio::io_context io;
    int ran = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
        boost::asio::post(io, [&ran] { ++ran; });
    }
    io.run();  // lint-run: the page's event loop, suspended into the browser's
    if (ran != 3) {
        std::puts("handler count mismatch");
        return 1;
    }
    std::puts("ran 3 handlers");
    return 0;
}

The same lane checks idle waits and animation callbacks under continuous ready work in Chrome. See Browser observations for its measurements and failure criteria.

The exit status

After a suspension, Asyncify loses the value main returns: a program whose exit status matters, under node, ends with std::exit; webcpp’s own tests end through webcpp::test::exit_status, and a test that does not fails (AGENTS.md chapter 9). asio’s tests pin both cases where node would read a failure as a pass, in each variant: a main that never finishes, and a main that suspended and then returns 1 without the helper.

TLS: build OpenSSL from source on native and WASI

For a program including <webcpp/asio/ssl.hpp>, add /webcpp/asio//openssl beside /webcpp/asio//asio in its target sources: exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/asio//asio /webcpp/asio//openssl ;. This forwards /webcpp/third_party//openssl, which builds OpenSSL 3.5.9 (commit 45e844fa2a14ec92d146bd8f5778ac130b6625fb) from the unmodified upstream submodule. No installed OpenSSL or OPENSSL_ROOT is used by this target.

In a Git checkout, initialize the source with git submodule update --init third_party/libs/openssl. A WebCPP source distribution already contains the required OpenSSL files and does not need Git. The build needs Python 3, Perl, Make, and the selected compiler toolchain; Git is also used to verify a source checkout. B2 invokes upstream Configure/Make and exports static libssl.a, libcrypto.a and their matching generated headers. Before Configure, it stages the distributable source files in a temporary directory and verifies their paths, file modes and content hashes against the pin. Missing, additional or altered files fail the build. Dot paths and pinned optional upstream repositories are omitted, just as in the source distribution. The temporary source directory also avoids upstream Makefiles’ restriction on source paths containing spaces. Different toolsets, optimization flags, exception settings and thread profiles use separate build directories. Effective C flags and compiler commands also identify separate archive/header directories. Flags retain normal B2 scope: dependency-specific cflags belong on the OpenSSL target, not only on its consumer. Independent concurrent B2 processes should use separate --build-dir directories. threading=single builds OpenSSL with no-threads; threading=multi enables its platform threading implementation. Native recipes support Clang/GCC on macOS/Linux and MSVC on Windows. MSVC uses upstream Configure and nmake, static archives and the B2 runtime/debug settings; the initial Windows recipe uses portable C without requiring NASM.

For a program built both natively and for the browser, use the condition below. It also selects OpenSSL for WASIp2/P3; browser builds retain the settings adapter:

project : requirements <conditional>@source-openssl ;

rule source-openssl ( properties * )
{
    if ! <toolset>emscripten in $(properties)
    {
        return <library>/webcpp/asio//openssl ;
    }
}

Do not use <toolset>!emscripten:<library>/webcpp/asio//openssl: that spelling silently fails to link OpenSSL in the tested B2 configuration.

Correct configuration errors as follows:

  • If ssl.hpp reports that OpenSSL is not linked, name the openssl target. Outside B2, define WEBCPP_ASIO_HAS_OPENSSL=1 and supply matching headers, libssl, libcrypto and platform dependencies yourself.

  • If the source checkout is missing, initialize the submodule with the command above. Tests requiring OpenSSL fail rather than silently skipping TLS.

  • If the target is named for the browser, select native or WASIp2/P3. The browser settings record does not implement TLS inside the Wasm module.

  • With WASIp3 threading=multi, use exception-handling=off with wasi-sdk 34.0: its cooperative sysroot does not contain the C++ exception runtime.

The built-in default and base providers are linked statically. Loading provider modules is disabled; this configuration is not a FIPS build. Both WASI profiles disable assembly, dynamic loading, QUIC, Unix-domain sockets and the OpenSSL thread pool. Native Clang/GCC builds retain upstream assembly optimizations; the initial MSVC recipe uses portable C. The recipe uses function and data sections plus platform dead stripping. A program has one OpenSSL provider. Native Trystero’s /webcpp/trystero//native target builds pinned static libdatachannel and its required nested sources against this same provider, so it can coexist with Asio and Beast. Such a program selects threading=multi and exceptions for Trystero’s worker-thread backend. Libsecp256k1 remains externally provisioned; OPENSSL_ROOT and LIBDATACHANNEL_ROOT do not select alternate providers.

The configured certificate directory is /etc/ssl. A source-built library does not install a system trust store or import the macOS keychain. Use the embedded factory in How-to: configure trusted certificate authorities for portable defaults, or explicitly load the intended CA file, set verify_peer, and verify the peer’s hostname on a raw context. WASI applications using a file must preopen its directory. Embedded authorities need no certificate filesystem access. Both require the needed TCP network capability; linking the library grants no runtime permission.

WASI seeding explicitly selects OpenSSL’s getrandom configuration, whose WASI implementation calls getentropy, then wasi-libc’s secure wasi:random/random.get-random-bytes host import. With Wasmtime’s default host configuration, the generator is seeded from the operating system. The host remains trusted: an embedder can replace its randomness provider. The tests verify that host entropy is requested and a reported entropy failure prevents random output and key generation; they do not prove cryptographic entropy quality or snapshot/restore safety. Reseed policy after restoring a seeded instance requires separate validation.

The reproducible native/WASIp3 test driver is python3 tools/openssl/test/run.py --fresh from the superproject. It needs Python with TLS 1.3 and an OpenSSL 3 command-line program only to create short-lived server fixtures. The client links the source-built library. WASMTIME selects the runtime executable; the recorded WASIp2/P3 checks use wasi-sdk 34.0 and Wasmtime 50.0.1. See Networking features for the target/variant matrix.

The recurring own lane b2 libs/asio/test/tls//tls-integration drives those TLS, embedded-CA, state, cancellation and entropy fixtures on native and WASIp3 profiles. The separate libs/asio/test/wasip2_tls_cobalt//wasip2-tls own lane drives the WASIp2 fixtures with both exception modes; see Build for WASIp2 for the complete command, including the ordinary Cobalt consumers. b2 libs/asio/test/tls//openssl-upstream is native only: it requests webcpp-openssl-tests=on, builds and runs upstream’s full alltests suite, then links a TLS consumer against those exact archives. The openssl-upstream-msvc-14.3 and openssl-upstream-msvc-14.5 aliases exercise that suite with the corresponding Windows CI toolsets. Ordinary consumers do not run that suite. The upstream harness is unavailable on WASI; the separate integration tests give narrower evidence and do not claim upstream-suite parity. A lane declaration is not evidence that the current candidate passed CI.

The library’s targets implement that distinction:

rule openssl-linked ( properties * )
{
    if [ webcpp-target.target-of $(properties) ] in native wasip2 wasip3
    {
        return <library>/webcpp/third_party//openssl
            <define>WEBCPP_ASIO_HAS_OPENSSL=1 ;
    }
}

# Refused on Emscripten: every source of a program built for emscripten
# that names it stops at the forced include, whose message says what to
# write. Quoted, as the Jamroot quotes Boost's directory, for a path that
# holds a space.
path-constant WEBCPP_ASIO_ROOT : . ;
alias openssl : : : : <conditional>@openssl-linked
    <toolset>emscripten:<cflags>"-include \"$(WEBCPP_ASIO_ROOT)/src/openssl_on_webassembly.hpp\""
    <toolset>emscripten:<cxxflags>"-include \"$(WEBCPP_ASIO_ROOT)/src/openssl_on_webassembly.hpp\"" ;

How-to: configure trusted certificate authorities

For a native or WASI client with portable trust defaults, include <webcpp/asio/tls_client_context.hpp> and link /webcpp/asio//tls. The target includes Asio, source-built OpenSSL and /webcpp/third_party//ca_certificates. No certificate file, environment setting, system trust store or network download is read by the factory. WASI needs no certificate directory preopen; a network connection still needs host permission.

This program prepares the context and checks errors without exceptions. With no arguments it uses the embedded roots. An optional argument supplies replacement PEM bytes, not a file path:

#include <cstdio>
#include <webcpp/asio/tls_client_context.hpp>
#include <webcpp/test/exit_status.hpp>

// main's standard signature requires char**, even though it does not modify argv.
// NOLINTNEXTLINE(misc-const-correctness)
int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    // An optional argument contains replacement PEM bytes, not a filename.
    // Keep the prepared context mutable for subsequent TLS stream construction.
    // NOLINTNEXTLINE(misc-const-correctness)
    auto prepared = argc == 1 ? webcpp::asio::make_tls_client_context()
                              : webcpp::asio::make_tls_client_context(argv[1]);
    if (!prepared) {
        const auto message = prepared.error().message();
        (void)std::fprintf(stderr, "%s\n", message.c_str());
        return webcpp::test::exit_status(1);
    }
    // Pass *prepared to TLS streams and keep it alive while those streams exist.
    std::puts(argc == 1 ? "TLS client ready: embedded authorities"
                        : "TLS client ready: replacement authorities");
    return webcpp::test::exit_status(0);
}

The default invocation prints:

TLS client ready: embedded authorities

Use the resulting context when constructing TLS streams and keep it alive while they exist. The factory enables verify_peer and requires TLS 1.2 or newer. Configure ssl::host_name_verification for the expected hostname and set SNI on each connection. A trusted issuer alone does not establish the intended hostname.

The overload taking std::string_view replaces the complete trust set. It does not append private authorities to public roots. Supply one or more PEM CA certificates separated by whitespace. Empty input, malformed certificates, non-CA certificates, and trailing non-whitespace data return an error without a usable context. The certificates are copied into the context; the input may then be released. Initialization failures are errors as values too, with or without exceptions. OpenSSL owns its allocations and does not use an Asio allocator. On Emscripten the helper returns unsupported_target: browser TLS and its trust policy remain under the browser’s control.

Updating the embedded snapshot

The source is the Mozilla CA export from curl, preserved in third_party/ca_certificates/cacert.pem with its MPL-2.0 license. The adjacent manifest records the source URL, date, SHA-256 and each certificate’s DER fingerprint. The initial snapshot is dated 2026-09-25 and contains 121 CAs. Keep its license and corresponding PEM source available when redistributing it.

Choose a published date from the curl CA Extract page. From the superproject root:

python3 tools/ca_certificates/update.py --date 2026-09-25
python3 tools/test/ca_certificates_test.py
python3 tools/test/ca_certificates_b2_test.py
python3 tools/ca_certificates/run.py --fresh

The updater downloads through verified HTTPS, checks the published SHA-256, validates every certificate and reports added/removed fingerprints. Review the trust changes and version the PEM and manifest together. An older date is rejected. Use --output DIRECTORY to stage a candidate separately, or --source-file PATH --sha256 DIGEST for an independently authenticated offline copy. A checksum detects a changed artifact; it is not an independent publisher signature. Normal builds use the pinned artifact without downloading anything.

Rebuild and redeploy applications after changing the snapshot. Existing binaries retain their embedded roots. The updater does not schedule downloads or alter running programs. The build rejects a missing or hash-mismatched snapshot. If an update was interrupted between replacing its two files, restore both from Git and repeat it. Run only one updater per output directory.

Using installed headers

b2 install --prefix=DIR includes the generated webcpp/asio/detail/ca_certificates.hpp under DIR/include/. Its private namespace is webcpp::asio::detail::ca_certificates. The matching PEM source, manifest and MPL notices are under DIR/include/webcpp/ca_certificates/. The CA package is generated locally without compiling OpenSSL. A consumer of the installed TLS header must still configure Boost, define WEBCPP_ASIO_HAS_OPENSSL=1 and link compatible OpenSSL headers and archives. Installation does not package the Cobalt runner or dependency archives.

What portable trust does and does not mean

The PEM export omits some additional constraints enforced by Firefox. It does not reproduce the complete browser policy, consult the host’s private roots or automatically fetch revocation information. Explicit replacement lets an application choose a narrower or organizational trust set. Native system trust integration and automatic runtime updates are separate features.

Local tests cover real TLS 1.2/1.3 connections, wrong hostnames, an unrelated CA, and rejection of a private test CA by the default public bundle. They also check complete replacement and invalid input. The matrix covers native macOS single/multi with exceptions on/off, WASIp2/P3 single with exceptions on/off, and WASIp3 cooperative threads with exceptions off under SDK 34. The WASIp3 client runs without certificate filesystem grants. Tests use a fresh local test CA; they do not depend on a public website’s availability.

Build for WASIp2

Use /webcpp/asio//asio with toolset=clang-wasip2 and threading=single. This profile uses Boost 1.92, wasi-sdk 34.0 and Wasmtime 50.0.1. Both exception modes are supported for the core, timers, TCP/UDP, asynchronous forward DNS, Cobalt and source-built OpenSSL. Multiple application threads remain unavailable with the pinned SDK profile.

Configure the compiler using the project’s wasi-sdk user-configuration example. Then run the local consumers from the superproject root:

b2 -a toolset=clang-wasip2 variant=release threading=single \
  exception-handling=on,off testing.launcher=tools/boost/asio-wasip2/run.sh \
  libs/asio/test/wasip2 libs/asio/test/capability_wasi
b2 -a toolset=clang-wasip2 variant=release exception-handling=on,off \
  libs/asio/test/wasip2//supplied-stream libs/asio/test/wasip2//scheduler-idle

Add /webcpp/asio//cobalt for Cobalt, //tls for OpenSSL with embedded or replacement trust roots, or //cobalt_ssl for Cobalt’s SSL wrapper. These targets share the same source-built provider as native and WASIp3 programs. Run their real peer, trust, transfer/shutdown and cancellation consumers with:

b2 -a toolset=clang-wasip2 variant=release exception-handling=on,off \
  testing.launcher=tools/boost/asio-wasip2/run.sh \
  libs/asio/test/wasip2_tls_cobalt libs/asio/test/wasip2_tls_cobalt//wasip2-tls

The first command exercises timers, the run/poll family, TCP and UDP exchanges, coroutines, forward name resolution and pollable readiness. The supplied-stream lane keeps standard input open without sending data; its timer must still cancel a pending read. Each consumer reports a passing result. The network launcher explicitly grants socket access and IP name lookup; production hosts should grant only the application’s required capabilities.

The idle driver uses an external watchdog and a Wasmtime fuel budget. A context with a live work guard must remain asleep, including before a reactor is created. The write-permit consumers exercise a real output with a controlled 64-bit quota and cancellation against a deliberately non-ready native pollable. Those fixtures test the adapter’s boundary handling; they do not measure every host implementation.

How readiness reaches the executor

WASIp2 provides TCP, UDP, name-resolution streams, monotonic clocks and resources that expose readiness through wasi:io/poll. The port retains Boost.Asio’s select reactor. wasi-libc gathers socket pollables and timer deadlines into one host wait. No worker thread, fixed-interval DNS scan or browser turn budget is introduced. The P2 single-thread profile omits Asio’s pipe-based cross-thread interrupter: this libc has no P2 pipe implementation, and the profile cannot receive work from another application thread. An idle scheduler without a reactor waits on a maximum-instant monotonic-clock pollable. It does not submit an empty poll list, which WASIp2 rejects, or spin.

A DNS address stream is not a POSIX descriptor. A small compiled bridge registers its borrowed pollable with wasi-libc’s descriptor table so the same reactor can wait for sockets, DNS and timers together. That registration API is private to wasi-libc. The build verifies SDK 34.0, libc revision 2e6fb9d8ee0c and the exact copied declaration hashes. Changing the SDK requires revalidating this bridge; the build must not silently use an unknown ABI. The upstream installation is never modified.

Resolver contract

async_resolve starts the native lookup through the executor. A deferred token does not start DNS until initiated. The handler never runs inside initiation, uses its associated executor, and receives an error value on failure. Resolver cancellation and per-operation cancellation work before and after registration. Destroying a resolver cancels pending lookups; destroying its context abandons handlers and releases the owned resources.

Numeric host parsing and the libc service-name table require no host DNS wait. The host supplies forward lookup addresses; host capabilities govern access. canonical_name, v4_mapped and all_matching are explicitly unsupported by this adapter and complete with operation_not_supported. Asynchronous reverse lookup also remains unsupported. address_configured uses libc’s numeric family checks. Loopback tests establish local resolution, not access to every external DNS server.

Operation storage and copied input/endpoint scratch storage use the associated handler allocator. Resolver ownership uses the context allocator. The public Boost result container, libc address parsing and descriptor-table storage retain their upstream allocation behavior; this is not a zero-global-allocation promise.

Use a supplied CLI byte stream

webcpp::asio::wasi::stdio_stream implements partial synchronous and asynchronous reads/writes over WASIp2 CLI resources. Its asynchronous waits use the same reactor, preserve completion-token associations and support cancellation. Only one read and one write may be pending per stream. Keep buffer storage alive until completion. The stream owns resource handles but does not close libc’s descriptors 0 and 1. Cancellation aborts pending operations; subsequent operations remain usable. Closing or destroying the stream cancels pending operations and prevents new I/O.

The Beast supplied-channel client and server run real WebSocket upgrade, text, fragmented binary transfer, ping/pong and close over this adapter, in both exception modes. They need no TCP socket grant. These channels do not provide Unix socket names, descriptor passing, peer credentials or wasi:http WebSocket upgrades.

Writes request a WASI flush before the protocol switches to reading. Readiness cannot preempt an import that the host itself implements with blocking I/O. In particular, Wasmtime CLI stdout can block when its OS pipe fills. A paused consumer must resume draining before the component can observe cancellation. A strict cancellation deadline requires a host/channel whose write imports remain nonblocking.

Unsupported operations and build profiles

threading=multi is rejected: SDK 34.0 has no supported P2 pthread runtime profile. POSIX signals, Unix-domain sockets and serial ports are absent from the host interfaces used here. Use the capability guards in Require a capability at compile time for compiler-visible requirements. Cobalt’s known no-EH pending-task move issue remains an upstream limitation, as on native and P3; see Exceptions and error handling.

Unsupported socket operations retain error-code overloads. Tested examples include linger and at_mark, which return operation_not_supported. UDP send_to and connected send gather multiple buffers into one datagram; receive scatters one datagram across the destination buffers. Asynchronous forms retain handler allocation and cancellation. TCP retains partial I/O semantics. Numeric IPv6 scope identifiers work; named interfaces are rejected with invalid_argument. Host permission denial is a runtime error, distinct from an unsupported build profile. Prefer error-code/completion-handler paths for recovery, especially when exception handling is disabled.

Build and test a WASIp3 program

This how-to uses the same timer example as the native tutorial. The port also provides TCP/UDP through Boost’s socket types. Read Target and variant capabilities before choosing a profile; it records the restrictions that still differ from native.

Prerequisites

Use Boost 1.92.0, wasi-sdk 34.0 and Wasmtime 50.0.1 for the configuration verified here. The port pins the exact input headers: a newer or modified Boost requires rebasing the patch and rerunning the tests. It is not accepted silently. WASIp3 and cooperative threads require runtime support; the previously installed Wasmtime 47.0.3 could not load the SDK’s cooperative-thread component.

Register clang-wasip3 in user-config.jam as shown by the superproject’s WASI setup. Put the SDK in .local/wasi-sdk, or supply -sWASI_SDK=/path/to/wasi-sdk when choosing the cooperative profile. It must be the same SDK as the compiler registered for this toolset. Put the tested Wasmtime binary on PATH.

/webcpp/asio//asio prepares a private copy of the patched Boost headers under bin/boost-asio-wasip3/include. It verifies the input and output hashes and searches those headers before the stock headers, only for clang-wasip3. It does not rewrite the Boost installation. Native and browser builds retain their existing headers and settings.

Run without threads

From the superproject root, build and check the existing timer example:

b2 -a toolset=clang-wasip3 variant=release threading=single \
  exception-handling=on \
  testing.launcher=tools/boost/asio-wasip3/run.sh \
  libs/asio/example//asio_quick_start.output

The example’s source is in Tutorial: your first asynchronous program. Expected output:

posted
timer fired
run returned 2 handlers

Repeat with exception-handling=off to use the single-thread runtime without C++ exceptions. The library keeps Boost’s callback and error-code interfaces. No JSPI or Asyncify flags are needed.

Run with cooperative threads

b2 -a toolset=clang-wasip3 variant=release threading=multi \
  exception-handling=off \
  testing.launcher=tools/boost/asio-wasip3/run.sh \
  libs/asio/test//wasi_core_threads

The build selects experimental-coop-threads as its sysroot and adds -pthread consistently to compilation and linking. It uses that sysroot’s C++ configuration and the matching SDK’s common libc++ headers. This is an experimental SDK profile, not a promise of CPU parallelism. In the tested SDK, requesting exceptions in this profile fails at configuration with a message naming the missing runtime.

The test launcher is for local and CI verification: it enables WASIp3 asynchronous components and cooperative-thread support, grants host network and name-lookup access for the loopback tests, and bounds each guest’s execution to 600 seconds. The global lane also runs large finite document and Unicode workloads. Set WEBCPP_WASIP3_TEST_TIMEOUT to a positive integer number of seconds to choose another bound, for example WEBCPP_WASIP3_TEST_TIMEOUT=15 for focused loopback tests. Invalid or zero bounds fail before launch. Enabling a runtime feature does not create threads in a single-thread binary. Production applications should choose their own timeout and network capabilities.

Reproduce the local verification

Run the declared WASIp3 tests and examples with -a, then repeat for each supported profile from Build configurations:

b2 -a toolset=clang-wasip3 variant=release threading=single \
  exception-handling=on \
  testing.launcher=tools/boost/asio-wasip3/run.sh \
  libs/asio/test libs/asio/example

b2 -a toolset=clang-wasip3 variant=release threading=single \
  exception-handling=off \
  testing.launcher=tools/boost/asio-wasip3/run.sh \
  libs/asio/test libs/asio/example

b2 -a toolset=clang-wasip3 variant=release threading=multi \
  exception-handling=off \
  testing.launcher=tools/boost/asio-wasip3/run.sh \
  libs/asio/test libs/asio/test//wasi_core_threads libs/asio/example

python3 tools/boost/asio-wasip3/prepare_test.py
python3 tools/test/asio_wasip3_test.py
python3 tools/boost/cobalt-wasip3/prepare_test.py
python3 tools/test/cobalt_wasip3_test.py

wasi_core exchanges real TCP and UDP traffic over ephemeral IPv4 loopback ports, tests timer and socket cancellation, scatter/gather TCP, and TCP EOF. wasi_core_threads adds a cross-thread post into a reactor with a pending timer and two runners sharing a context. wasi_contract checks empty datagrams, vectored UDP receive with datagram truncation, IPv6 numeric scopes, socket option errors and resolver behavior. wasi_coroutine waits for a timer using Boost.Asio’s co_spawn and awaitable with result-based error handling. The existing run-family and timer tests also run on WASIp3. wasi_udp_gather and capability_wasi/datagrams check synchronous and asynchronous multi-buffer sends and receives, including complete sequences beyond 64 buffers, allocation routing, empty datagrams, oversized input and release of storage before completion.

The preparation tests check exact hashes, idempotence and protection of the installed headers. The build tests use a checkout with spaces, check that the private headers are selected only for WASIp3, and reject unavailable SDK profiles. Native controls use the same runtime test sources. These are local commands; none starts a CI job.

Build a Cobalt application

Use <library>/webcpp/asio//cobalt in the application’s B2 requirements. Its ordinary boost::cobalt::main co_main(int, char**) entry point is unchanged. The target builds Boost.Cobalt from source, applies the checked Cobalt and Asio compatibility overlays, and supplies the signal-free WASIp3 runner. Applications do not compile a special subset of Cobalt sources themselves.

Run the existing Cobalt timer example:

b2 -a toolset=clang-wasip3 variant=release threading=single \
  exception-handling=on \
  testing.launcher=tools/boost/asio-wasip3/run.sh \
  libs/asio/example//asio_cobalt.output
cobalt slept

Repeat with exception-handling=off, or with threading=multi and exception-handling=off for the cooperative runtime. The latter can also run the explicit libs/asio/test//cobalt_thread test. The ordinary test target includes cobalt_wasi, cobalt_network_wasi and cobalt_io; they cover the runner, both timer APIs, Asio TCP/UDP through use_op, Cobalt’s own IP socket wrappers, refused TCP connections, TCP/UDP cancellation, EOF and result-based resolver behavior.

The libs/asio/test//cobalt_wasip3 lane checks successful and unsuccessful command completion with an exact-status driver. Put Wasmtime 50.0.1 on PATH, or set WASMTIME to its executable for that driver. The SDK maps nonzero coroutine returns to host status 1.

For TLS, add /webcpp/asio//tls and await Asio SSL operations with boost::cobalt::use_op. tools/openssl/test//cobalt_tls_client is a compiled consumer of both public targets. Run the following command to check TLS 1.2/1.3, trusted and rejected identities, malformed CA data and clean shutdown; the path is printed by B2’s link action:

python3 tools/openssl/test/tls.py <path-to-cobalt_tls_client> --embedded

The WASI client needs network capabilities but no CA filesystem preopen. To use Cobalt’s own io::ssl::stream, link the optional /webcpp/asio//cobalt_ssl target. Its checked patch, trust configuration and local test commands are described in How to use Cobalt’s SSL stream.

The underlying platform contracts are documented by wasi-sdk’s cooperative-thread guide and the Wasmtime release used here.

The run family

The io_context’s run, run_one, run_for, run_until, run_one_for and run_one_until keep Boost.Asio’s meaning on every target: run returns when the io_context is out of work or stopped, run_one after one handler, run_for and run_until after their deadline is observed, and each returns the number of handlers it ran. poll and poll_one are Boost’s everywhere. Natively the six are Boost’s own, and the options change nothing.

On emscripten the six hide Boost’s, and run is a composition of Boost’s own calls, which repeats four steps:

  1. Call poll_one until it returns 0 or max_handlers_per_turn handlers have run: a turn of the handlers that are ready.

  2. If the io_context is stopped, return.

  3. If the turn reached the limit, yield to the browser and go to step 1.

  4. Otherwise call Boost’s run_one, which suspends in the reactor’s select until a timer, a post or I/O makes a handler ready, and runs it. If it ran none, the io_context being stopped or out of work, return; else go to step 1.

run_for and run_until are the same composition with Boost’s run_one_until in step 4. Like Boost’s, they check their deadline before each handler, so that a deadline already passed runs nothing, and they return once it has passed, even when every turn reaches the limit. A running handler cannot be interrupted, and host scheduling can delay resumption beyond the deadline. run_one is step 4 alone, and run_one_for and run_one_until are Boost’s, each running one handler at most. Code that calls run through a boost::asio::io_context& gets Boost’s own run, which suspends as well but has no limit.

A turn at a time

Boost’s run runs handlers until none is ready, those posted meanwhile included, and a select whose timeout is zero suspends only to a microtask, which never lets the page render. Measured with Emscripten 6.0.11, a handler that posts itself ran 300,000 times under Boost’s run before a JavaScript setTimeout(0) ran, in either suspension variant. Boost’s run is not virtual and cannot be told to yield, hence the composition.

The yield is a suspension, an EM_ASYNC_JS import whose promise a MessageChannel message resolves: a macrotask rather than only a microtask, giving the browser an opportunity to render, run timers and deliver events. It does not guarantee that any particular work happens before the next turn. MessageChannel exists in every browser and in node.

A turn runs at most max_handlers_per_turn handlers, and the run family yields to the browser after each turn that reaches it. Step 4’s one handler belongs to no turn: when it follows a short turn of k handlers and its wait ends at once, a timer having fallen due meanwhile, no macrotask comes between them, so that up to k + 1 + max_handlers_per_turn handlers, at most twice the limit, can run between two yields. The option is 100 by default. Historically, with a limit of 1000 and Emscripten 6.0.11, the setTimeout(0) above ran after 1,000 handlers under JSPI and 999 under Asyncify, against 300,000 without the limit, and run still ran every handler. It is given at construction, io_context io(io_context_options{.max_handlers_per_turn = 250}), or later with io.max_handlers_per_turn(250); 0 is taken as 1. A stop made by the handler that reaches the limit returns at once, without a yield first. Held by turn_limit, which counts the yields of a handler that posts itself: one after every max_handlers_per_turn handlers under run and run_for, never more handlers between two, and none under Boost’s own run; and a JavaScript setTimeout(0) runs at a yield, seen by the first handler of a turn. And by run_family, in each variant.

Configure the build’s default turn limit

WEBCPP_ASIO_DEFAULT_MAX_HANDLERS_PER_TURN in config.hpp supplies the initial value of io_context_options::max_handlers_per_turn. It defaults to 100 and can be replaced by a compiler definition, for example to use 1000:

-DWEBCPP_ASIO_DEFAULT_MAX_HANDLERS_PER_TURN=1000

For b2, pass the definition on the command line for the complete build:

b2 -a --build-dir=bin/asio-limit-1000 toolset=emscripten \
    define=WEBCPP_ASIO_DEFAULT_MAX_HANDLERS_PER_TURN=1000 \
    libs/asio/example//asio_cobalt.output

Use the same value in every translation unit that uses asio and rebuild all of them when changing it. In particular, Cobalt’s runner is compiled separately: a definition in an application source file alone cannot configure an existing runner archive. A separate build directory avoids reusing outputs built with another definition. Do not mix differently configured objects in one program.

An explicit option at construction or a later max_handlers_per_turn(n) call overrides this build default for that context. Zero is normalized to one; negative build defaults are rejected. Native scheduling is unchanged.

The value 100 is a configurable scheduling policy, not a measured optimum or a time budget. Smaller values offer more frequent yields under continuous ready work, with more suspension and scheduling overhead. A single expensive handler can still block the thread. The original browser measurements used small self-posting handlers and checked turn duration, not isolated yield cost. The later Release benchmark measures yield latency separately. See From the original 1,000 default to 100 for the default’s origin and validation, and Relating the limit to an application’s cost budget for the cost model and its limits.

Who may call it

The run family is called on the stack of main, or on the stack of another export the program lists for suspension: in -sJSPI_EXPORTS under JSPI, whose call then returns a promise, and called with ccall(..., {async: true}) under Asyncify. Anywhere else its first suspension fails: under JSPI it throws a SuspendError, and under Asyncify it starts an unwind that corrupts a suspended main. Nothing calls run, poll or dispatch from a JavaScript event: while run is suspended, an event sees running_in_this_thread() true, because the frame run pushed stays on the stack, and a dispatch there runs its handler inside the event, on the wrong stack. asio’s bridge only posts. Nor does a program block the page’s thread without suspending, in a busy loop or a blocking system call.

On emscripten, a run family call made while another runs, or while the bridge delivers a browser event, asserts and returns 0 having run nothing. The io_context keeps a flag while one of its six members runs, and the bridge counts the deliveries in progress. A call while either is set (a nested call from a handler, a run from a JavaScript event while run waits, a run from a registration’s deliver) is a precondition violation, reported by BOOST_ASSERT_MSG, and with assertions off it is still refused. The run around a refused call goes on, still flagged. A handler’s C++ exception that leaves run clears the flag on its way, so that the program’s restart(); run(); after its catch is no nested call. A JavaScript error is another matter (see a JavaScript error out of a handler): where it skips destructors it leaves the flag set, as it leaves Boost’s own state broken, and the context refuses every later call. Each member admits its call once, before any work, and then runs only private code or Boost’s, never another member of the family, whose admission would refuse the call its caller flagged.

Detection is of a call of this run family on the context whose flag or bridge is set. Four calls go undetected: a call from an export of the program’s own that is not listed for suspension, which nothing tells from main until its first suspension fails; a call through a boost::asio::io_context&, which reaches Boost’s own run; poll, poll_one and dispatch, which are Boost’s and no member of the run family, called from a JavaScript event; and a call on another io_context, whose flag and bridge are its own, from a handler or a delivery of this one.

Held by detection, in each variant, with and without exceptions, with an assertion handler counting the assertions and with assertions off: a nested run_for, run_one and the other timed forms nested one after another in a single run, a run from a JavaScript setTimeout while run waits, a run from a delivery while no run is active and a handler is ready, which it leaves for the next run, run again after a C++ exception left it, every timed form over several turns and on a timer alone with no assertion, and the poll of a context with no reactor from a handler. And by flag_scope, the flag’s scope, which puts back the value it found.

A library never calls the run family: it is given an executor. webcpp’s lint refuses a call of run, run_one or run_for on an io_context whose line does not say why after lint-run:, and a program’s own says it, as io.run(); // lint-run: the program's event loop, suspended into the browser's.

xactor’s asio_driver drains an io_context of its own with poll. That context makes no timer and no socket, so it has no reactor: its poll never reaches select and never suspends, and calling it from a handler of the program’s io_context is safe in either variant.

Exceptions

A handler’s exception propagates out of run, as Boost’s, on both variants. Handlers run on the stack of main, inside the run family call, so that a C++ exception a handler throws leaves run, clearing the run family’s flag on its way, and reaches the program’s catch, after any number of suspensions and yields. A suspension keeps what encloses it: a try around run catches what a handler throws after run suspended, and a run called inside a catch block suspends and resumes there. Each variant compiles with the exception model it can suspend through (see the two suspension variants): WebAssembly exceptions under JSPI, and JavaScript-based exceptions under Asyncify, which traps when it suspends inside a catch block of WebAssembly exceptions. A JavaScript error out of a handler is caught by no C++ catch, and what it leaves depends on the build (see a JavaScript error out of a handler).

Held by exceptions, natively and in each variant, built with exceptions whatever the build asks: a try that encloses a run which suspends in the reactor’s wait catches nothing, a run suspends inside a catch block and resumes there, a handler’s exception thrown after run suspended reaches a catch in main, and the next run after it runs its handler, no nested call, and so does one thrown after run yielded twice to the browser, 2,000 handlers having filled two turns of the default limit.

Before run, and after main

On emscripten, handlers run only on the stack of a run family call, as natively: work posted before run is called waits for it, and a browser event that arrives while no run is active is posted and waits for the next one. Held by reactor, where work posted before run runs only inside it, and a post made from a JavaScript setTimeout wakes a suspended run.

As natively, run returns when no operation is pending, even with a connection open: a WebSocket with no pending read does not keep run alive, and its messages queue. After main returns, the runtime stays alive, since Emscripten keeps it by default, events keep being posted, and nothing runs them unless an export listed for suspension calls the run family again.

How to configure the turn limit

When ready work repeatedly posts more work, set the limit on the context that runs it. This program requests turns of 250 handlers and posts a finite chain of 5,000 pieces of work:

#include <webcpp/asio/io_context.hpp>

#include <webcpp/test/exit_status.hpp>

#include <boost/asio/post.hpp>

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <functional>

namespace asio = webcpp::asio;

namespace {

/** The context and remaining work of a finite chain of posted handlers. */
struct work {
    asio::io_context& io;
    std::size_t remaining;
};

/** Runs one piece of work and schedules the next without calling it inline. */
void next(work* state) {
    if (--state->remaining != 0) {
        boost::asio::post(state->io, std::bind_front(&next, state));
    }
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    asio::io_context io(asio::io_context_options{.max_handlers_per_turn = 250});
    work state{.io = io, .remaining = 5000};
    boost::asio::post(io, std::bind_front(&next, &state));
    std::printf("max_handlers_per_turn: %zu\n", io.max_handlers_per_turn());
    const auto handlers = io.run();  // lint-run: main owns the program's event loop
    std::printf("handlers run: %zu\n", handlers);
    return webcpp::test::exit_status(0);
}

Run it from the superproject root:

b2 toolset=emscripten libs/asio/example//asio_turn_limit.output
max_handlers_per_turn: 250
handlers run: 5000

Keep the state alive until run returns. Each handler posts the next one instead of calling it inline, so the context can yield between turns. Natively the same program prints the same output, but the option does not change Boost’s scheduling. Change the limit to trade handler throughput against opportunities for the browser to process other work. A handler that itself blocks for a long time still blocks the page; the option does not impose a time budget on individual handlers. The measured browser checks are described in Browser observations.

Measured cost of yielding to the browser

On 2026-10-15, a direct round trip through the library’s actual webcpp_asio_yield() took about 4.06 microseconds with JSPI and 4.74 microseconds with Asyncify. These are medians of seven per-run means, not the duration of a batch of callbacks and not a real-time guarantee. One microsecond is 0.001 milliseconds.

The benchmark ran locally on an Apple M5 Max, 128 GiB RAM, macOS 27.0 (26A428), HeadlessChrome 153.0.8010.12, Emscripten 6.0.11 and Boost 1.92. Both compilation and linking used Release -O3; NDEBUG was enabled. The primary matrix enabled exceptions and cross-origin isolation. Additional cases disabled exceptions or isolation and exercised an arithmetic workload. No CI ran. The benchmark used explicit limits; the configured default was 1,000 at measurement time. The subsequent policy decision below changes it to 100.

From the original 1,000 default to 100

The value 1,000 predates the isolated yield-cost benchmark. It was specified as the initial scheduling policy in design decision D3 and the implementation plan. The design recorded a timer witness: with that limit, setTimeout(0) ran after about 1,000 handlers instead of waiting for the entire ready chain. That establishes that yielding happens; it does not derive an optimal limit. No calculation selecting 1,000 over all other limits was recorded there.

Task 13 subsequently checked whether keeping that value was acceptable for its trivial-handler workload. Its local Chrome experiment measured full 1,000-handler turns in three debug runs on 2026-10-14. The p95 was 0.7 ms for JSPI and 1.6 ms for Asyncify in every run. Animation callbacks occurred about 60 times per second; the unbounded controls had none during the observed work. The measured maxima were 1.8-1.9 ms and 8.9-9.2 ms, respectively. These are historical batch durations, distinct from the Release yield latencies below. The complete historical table remains in the library’s AGENTS.md.

The predeclared stop criterion was a turn p95 above 8 ms in either variant. Its motivation was to leave roughly half of a 60 Hz frame’s 16.7 ms interval for browser work. This is a screening heuristic, not a guarantee of frame rate: p95 does not bound every turn, browser work varies, and an animation callback does not prove that particular pixels were painted. The observations passed that criterion, so the existing default was retained.

The 2026-10-15 Release benchmark then measured the missing part: the actual cost of yielding. It supports amortizing that cost across cheap callbacks; it does not retrospectively turn 1,000 into a mathematically derived optimum. The documented rationale is therefore: an initial configurable policy, retained after a workload-specific responsiveness check, with its scheduling cost now measured independently. Choosing an optimal default would require an explicit responsiveness/overhead objective and representative workloads across the supported browsers and hardware.

On 2026-10-15, after reviewing these results, the owner selected 100 as the new default to favor browser responsiveness. In a continuously ready chain, it offers roughly ten times as many yields as 1,000. The measured boundary gaps imply about 44.0/54.5 ms of accumulated scheduling time per million handlers at 100 (JSPI/Asyncify), versus 4.64/5.73 ms at 1,000. The additional 39/49 ms is an extrapolation from this machine, not one uninterrupted pause.

For illustration, 100 callbacks that each take 50 us occupy about 5 ms, whereas 1,000 occupy about 50 ms, excluding scheduling overhead. These are calculated examples, not measured application response times. Browser work gets an opportunity at a yield, not a guarantee that an input or frame runs before Wasm resumes. A long handler is never preempted; short-drain/wait paths can also run up to twice the configured count between yields, as described in The run family. The choice of 100 is a responsiveness-oriented policy, not proof of an optimum. Applications can still select 1,000 or another value.

What was timed

The direct measurement surrounds the production function without changing its implementation. The C++ steady-clock timestamp is read immediately before the call and immediately after it resumes. Their difference in milliseconds is multiplied by 1,000 to report microseconds. The compiled implementation is in bench/yield/yield_program.cpp.

That function awaits a Promise, creates a MessageChannel, posts a message, closes port1 in its message handler and resolves the Promise. The suspended Wasm execution then resumes. This is a cooperative browser event-loop yield, not a measurement of an operating-system thread context switch.

The chain measurement uses boost::asio::post to schedule its next handler. It records the end of the last callback before a yield, after posting its successor, and the entry of the first callback after the yield. This excludes batch execution, but includes the small dispatcher return/reentry around the yield. A matched control records the same boundaries with periodic yielding disabled. It uses exactly the same number of handlers and clock reads.

Each primary row contains seven fresh-page runs of 10,000 yields each. Percentiles are nearest-rank quantiles per run, then medians across runs. The maximum is the largest individual observation across all repetitions. The mean range exposes variation between independent runs.

The amortized columns divide the measured gap by the turn limit. They are an estimate of scheduling cost per handler, not the handler’s execution time. For example, one million handlers with a limit of 1 imply roughly four to five seconds of accumulated yield gaps at these means. A limit of 100 implies roughly 44-55 milliseconds; a limit of 1,000 roughly 5-6 milliseconds. These extrapolations describe this workload and machine, not all applications.

The largest chain gaps were 5.01 ms with JSPI and 39.72 ms with Asyncify, both at limit 1. No samples were removed. The benchmark does not identify whether these outliers came from collection, scheduling or another cause. A browser yield gives an opportunity to service the page; it does not guarantee that rendering or a particular queued task executes before resumption.

Where the instrumented interval was spent

A separate run observes six JavaScript timestamps inside the MessageChannel path. The observer is warmed before collection. These observations perturb the operation: the median mean rises from 4.06 to 4.85 us for JSPI and from 4.74 to 5.57 us for Asyncify. Consequently the following decomposition is of the instrumented path, not a claim that the observer is free.

All entries below are arithmetic means across seven runs of 10,000 samples; they add to the arithmetic mean of the traced round trip. Sub-resolution values are aggregate estimates, not individually resolved durations.

Clock resolution and synchronous controls

In this Emscripten build, C++ steady_clock reaches clock_gettime, WASI’s monotonic clock and then emscripten_get_now, which uses performance.now(). C++ system_clock reaches the same wall-clock source as Date.now(). These are not independent hardware clocks. Two thousand bracketed reads before and after each Wasm case verified their correspondence.

Observed positive clock steps were about 5 us in an isolated page and 100 us in an ordinary page. Date.now() advanced in 1 ms steps where a positive step was observed. Isolated-page direct yield samples therefore include many zeros despite a nonzero aggregate mean. In an ordinary page, about 96% of JSPI and 95% of Asyncify direct samples were zero; the median p95 was also zero. Those individual percentiles cannot resolve a 4-5 us operation. The ordinary-page mean still agreed: 4.03 us JSPI and 4.73 us Asyncify.

What the measurements justify

For the instrumented trivial chain, limit 1 took 17.29 times the matched no-periodic-yield control with JSPI and 14.49 times with Asyncify. At limit 100 the ratios were 2.09 and 1.43; at limit 1,000 they were 1.15 and 1.05. These are measured whole-program ratios, including the clocks in both cases, not universal application overhead factors.

Subtracting whole-run durations is unreliable for small differences. Some large-limit pairs produced negative differences. Exception-free Asyncify’s large-limit controls were consistently slower than the yielding runs. This experiment does not identify the cause; execution/tiering, allocation and other runtime effects can confound such controls. The retained CSV and JSON include these results. They must not be described as negative yield latency. The direct interval and callback-boundary observations remain the primary latency measurements.

The evidence supports amortizing yields when handlers are very cheap. It does not prove that 1,000 is optimal, or that 1 is always inappropriate. A heavy handler can make a 4-5 us yield negligible. Choosing a limit balances accumulated scheduling cost against time spent away from the browser. Counting handlers cannot bound that time when their costs vary, and no limit interrupts a handler in the middle. Configure the limit as described in How to configure the turn limit; the current default is 100.

Relating the limit to an application’s cost budget

For a continuously ready chain with roughly uniform callbacks, let Y be mean yield latency, C the mean cost of handling one callback without a forced yield, and N the number of callbacks per turn. The scheduling cost per callback is approximately Y / N. Relative to the callback work, the added cost is approximately Y / (N * C). These are workload estimates, not latency bounds; they omit variability and other browser work.

For an allowed additional cost ratio r, the estimate asks for N >= Y / (r * C), rounded up to a positive integer. This must be balanced against time away from the browser, approximately N * C for this continuous chain. The general run-family paths described in A turn at a time can have more than one turn’s handlers between yields, and no handler is preempted.

For illustration only, assume Y = 5 us and allow 10% added scheduling cost:

A limit of 1 can be inexpensive for substantial callbacks; 1,000 can amortize scheduling for extremely cheap callbacks. Conversely, 1,000 callbacks that each take 100 us can occupy the thread for about 100 ms before a periodic yield in this chain. Measure the actual application and choose its limit using the build definition or the per-context option.
