Reproduce and inspect

The manual benchmark is in bench/yield/; its README documents exact build, run and analysis commands. It is not connected to a CI lane. The recorded results/2026-10-15/runs.csv retains statistics for every case, summary.json groups repetitions, and build.json identifies the hardware, toolchain and source/binary hashes. Full timestamp arrays are also preserved in the local raw-data archive identified in the README.

The run used 442 sequential fresh-page cases in deterministic shuffled order (seed 20261015), totaling 970,139,132 operations and 9,429,856 timing pairs. Primary cases had seven repetitions; secondary controls had three. Direct and chain Wasm cases first warmed 512 actual yields, and chain cases additionally warmed 10,001 posted handlers. Builds completed before measurement started. There was no polling timer in the measured page. The machine was not isolated from all other OS activity, and this headless, otherwise idle-page experiment does not represent a loaded application’s rendering or input workload.

Browser events

On emscripten every event source of asio and of the libraries built on it, a WebSocket’s onmessage, a fetch promise, a WebRTC callback, is a JavaScript function made by the io_context’s bridge, webcpp::asio::browser::bridge. The bridge is a service of the io_context, Boost.Asio’s own mechanism, so that it is made with the context’s allocator, on first use, and shut down and destroyed with the context. From the test bridge, where two events delivered before run wait for it:

webcpp::asio::io_context io;
counter listener(io, 0);  // a registration, which posts each event it receives
auto& bridge = boost::asio::use_service<webcpp::asio::browser::bridge>(io);
const std::uint64_t key = bridge.add(listener);
const emscripten::val deliver = bridge.function(key);  // for JavaScript to call
deliver(1);
deliver(2);
BOOST_TEST_EQ(listener.received, 0);  // posted, and waiting for run
BOOST_TEST_EQ(io.run(), 2U);          // lint-run: the test's event loop
BOOST_TEST_EQ(listener.received, 2);
bridge.remove(key);

A registration is what an event delivered through the bridge reaches: an object of a class derived from webcpp::asio::browser::registration, owned and allocated by whoever adds it, an operation, a stream or a channel. Its deliver is given the event and returns whether the registration is done, in which case the bridge removes it; its shutdown is the context’s shutdown, which destroys what is pending without calling it. The bridge keeps a pointer to each, by key, in a map allocated with the context’s allocator. Natively there is no bridge: browser/ builds on emscripten alone.

A browser event delivered through the bridge only posts; a listener is no outstanding work. A registration’s deliver posts what the event completes or notifies to the io_context, and does nothing else: it never polls, runs or dispatches. The post wakes a suspended run through the reactor, and an event that arrives while no run is active is posted and waits for the next one. A registered listener keeps no run alive: run returns when nothing is pending, as natively a socket with no pending operation does not keep it.

Posting is the only choice. While run is suspended in the reactor’s select, the frame that Boost’s scheduler pushed for it stays on the call stack, so that an event sees running_in_this_thread() true, and boost::asio::dispatch called there runs its handler at once, inside the event and on its stack, rather than on the stack of run (measured with Emscripten 6.0.11). And calling the run family from an event fails at its first suspension: under JSPI it throws a SuspendError, and under Asyncify it starts an unwind that corrupts the suspended main (see Who may call it). Under Asyncify a wake must also come from JavaScript with no compiled code on the stack, which a post gives. So an event may call what returns at once without suspending, which posting is, and no member of the run family, nor poll, poll_one or dispatch. While it delivers, the bridge says so, delivering(), so that the run family can refuse a call made from inside a delivery. Only the bridge’s own JavaScript functions deliver, and they count the deliveries in progress, nested ones included, which delivering() reads. Through the bridge, a program can neither deliver outside that count, deliver being private, nor change it, delivering() taking no value; the export those functions call is the JavaScript boundary’s, declared in a detail header, and calling it from C++ is outside the contract.

A registration’s key is never reused; an event of a removed key, or of a destroyed io_context, finds nothing. Keys are std::uint64_t values counted from 1, which JavaScript holds as a BigInt, so that no count of registrations a program reaches wraps around. Each function the bridge makes carries its key and a token that the bridge clears at its shutdown: an event of a key the bridge no longer holds delivers nothing, and an event that arrives after the io_context was destroyed does not reach WebAssembly at all. A registration must outlive its key, and is removed before it is destroyed; the context’s shutdown calls the shutdown of each registration still held.

An exception that escapes a delivery, a C++ exception from a registration’s deliver or a JavaScript error from a function it calls, is caught at the bridge’s boundary and reported with the page’s reportError, or console.error where there is none, and the event that raised it is lost. A C++ exception is caught in C++, which frees its object: one that reached the page would keep it for good. A JavaScript error passes every C++ catch and leaves WebAssembly without running its frames’ epilogues, in every build; it runs their destructors in a build with WebAssembly exceptions, the JSPI variant’s, and skips them with JavaScript exceptions, the Asyncify variant’s, and without exceptions (measured with Emscripten 6.0.11). So the JavaScript side of the boundary keeps what must hold however a delivery ends: it puts WebAssembly’s stack pointer back where it was before the call, puts the count of deliveries in progress back, and frees the event’s handle, which C++ only borrows. Where destructors are skipped, what the registration’s own frames owned is not freed: a registration that calls JavaScript which may throw catches the error there.

What the boundary does not catch is the runtime’s own. A trap, a WebAssembly.RuntimeError, which Emscripten’s abort() throws too, goes on to the page after the stack pointer is put back, as it does from any other call into WebAssembly, rather than being reported and swallowed as an error of the program’s; and the ExitStatus that exit() throws, or Emscripten’s 'unwind', ends the delivery without a report, as Emscripten’s own callbacks do. A handler’s exception is another matter: it is thrown by a handler that run runs, on the stack of main, and propagates out of run, as Boost’s does.

A JavaScript error that a handler lets escape crosses no boundary of asio’s: it leaves run, and the page’s JavaScript may catch it around a call of an export listed for suspension and call that export again. With WebAssembly exceptions the frames it leaves run their destructors, Boost’s and asio’s, and the next run runs as after a C++ exception. With JavaScript exceptions, and without exceptions, the destructors are skipped and the context is left broken whatever asio does. Boost’s scheduler keeps the finished handler’s work counted, so that Boost’s own run, reached through a boost::asio::io_context&, never returns once out of work. Boost’s call stack keeps the frame run pushed, so that running_in_this_thread() is true outside any run, and a dispatch anywhere runs its handler at once. And the run family’s flag stays set, so that every later call asserts and returns 0. No boundary can put Boost’s state back, since the frames that would are the ones the error skips, so asio does not put its flag back either: a refusal reports the broken context where a run that never returns would not. A handler that calls JavaScript which may throw catches the error in JavaScript, as a registration does. (Measured with Emscripten 6.0.11 in both variants, with exceptions and without: an export listed for suspension runs the context, a handler’s JavaScript error escapes it, the page catches the error and calls the export again.)

Held by bridge, in each variant, with exceptions and without them: an event posts and wakes run; events delivered before run wait for it; a listener and nothing pending let run return; a registration that is done is removed; an event of a removed key, and one of a destroyed io_context, find nothing, and the context’s destruction shuts its registrations down; 3,000 C++ exceptions, and 3,000 JavaScript errors, escaping deliveries called in a row from JavaScript are each reported, with the stack pointer where it was, as many Emval handles as before, and the bridge no longer delivering; a delivery dispatched from inside another, ending normally or with a JavaScript error, leaves the outer one delivering; and a trap goes on to the caller while 'unwind' and an ExitStatus pass unreported. By bridge_deliver_refused and bridge_set_delivering_refused, where a program that calls the bridge’s deliver, or gives delivering() a value, fails to compile, beside bridge_private, which compiles. And by em_js, which loads every JavaScript function of asio and of its tests, so that one that does not parse fails before main.

Promises and events

Tutorial: receive a value and a rejection

On Emscripten, browser::async_await connects a JavaScript Promise to an Asio executor. Build this example with b2 toolset=emscripten libs/asio/example//asio_promise.output.

#include <cstdio>
#include <webcpp/asio/browser/async_await.hpp>
#include <webcpp/asio/io_context.hpp>
#include <webcpp/test/exit_status.hpp>

int main() {
    webcpp::asio::io_context io;
    auto resolved = emscripten::val::global("Promise").call<emscripten::val>("resolve", 42);
    auto rejected = emscripten::val::global("Promise").call<emscripten::val>("reject", 9);
    int failures = 0;
    webcpp::asio::browser::async_await(
        io.get_executor(), resolved,
        [&](boost::system::error_code ec, const emscripten::val& value) {
            if (ec) {
                ++failures;
                return;
            }
            std::printf("resolved: %d\n", value.as<int>());
        });
    webcpp::asio::browser::async_await(
        io.get_executor(), rejected,
        [&](boost::system::error_code ec, const emscripten::val& reason) {
            if (ec != webcpp::asio::browser::error::promise_rejected) {
                ++failures;
                return;
            }
            std::printf("rejected: promise_rejected %d\n", reason.as<int>());
        });
    io.run();  // lint-run: main waits for both Promise completions
    return webcpp::test::exit_status(failures);
}

Expected output:

resolved: 42
rejected: promise_rejected 9

A callback receives an error code and an emscripten::val: success supplies the resolved value, and promise_rejected supplies the rejection reason. Embind is linked by the library’s build requirements.

How-to: choose a completion token or cancel a wait

Callbacks, boost::asio::deferred, boost::asio::use_awaitable and boost::cobalt::use_op use the same initiation. Coroutine tokens that turn errors into exceptions require exception support for that error path. Use an error-preserving completion token adapter for errors as values.

Bind a cancellation slot to the handler and emit terminal, partial or total to complete the wait with operation_aborted and undefined. none does nothing. Completion is posted, never invoked inside initiation or the cancellation signal. The Promise itself continues running; any late settlement finds no registration and cannot complete the operation again.

Reference: values, ownership and allocation

The completion signature is void(boost::system::error_code, emscripten::val). The rejection category is webcpp.asio, with value 1 and message the promise was rejected. JavaScript Promise.resolve normalizes inputs: an ordinary value is accepted, and already-settled Promises still complete asynchronously. An undefined rejection reason is preserved.

A pending operation owns outstanding work. A Promise that never settles keeps run waiting until cancellation. Destroying the context destroys its pending handler without invoking it; later settlements are ignored. Operation storage uses the handler’s associated allocator, while the bridge service and its map use the context’s allocator. The operation preserves the executor’s concrete type when passed directly, including its scheduling properties. An explicitly type-erased any_io_executor remains accepted, but Boost’s erased executor can allocate its dispatch wrappers independently of the handler allocator. Custom executors likewise control their own storage. For the measured allocation guarantee, pass io.get_executor() directly. See Allocation.

Explanation: why the bridge posts the result

JavaScript delivers the settlement through Browser events. The bridge posts completion so application code runs on the event-loop stack, where suspension is supported. It never calls the handler inline from a Promise reaction. See guarantees [asio-invariant-10] and [asio-invariant-11].

Await one browser event

browser::async_wait_event(executor, target, type, token) completes with the next event of the requested type. It uses a one-shot listener and posts the event to the executor. The event type is copied into a JavaScript string, including when initiation is deferred; the view needs no terminating null. A pending wait owns work. Terminal, partial or total cancellation removes the listener and posts operation_aborted with undefined; none does nothing. Context destruction removes the listener and destroys the handler silently. Storage follows the same allocator and executor rules as Promise waits.

Tutorial: receive a message

This example creates an EventTarget, waits for its next message, and schedules a JavaScript timer to send it. Build with b2 toolset=emscripten libs/asio/example//asio_event.output.

#include <emscripten/em_js.h>
#include <cstdio>
#include <webcpp/asio/browser/async_wait_event.hpp>
#include <webcpp/asio/io_context.hpp>
#include <webcpp/test/exit_status.hpp>

// clang-format off
EM_JS(void, send_event, (emscripten::EM_VAL handle), {
    const target = Emval.toValue(handle);
    setTimeout(() => target.dispatchEvent(
        new CustomEvent('message', {detail: 5})), 20);
});
// clang-format on

int main() {
    webcpp::asio::io_context io;
    const auto target = emscripten::val::global("EventTarget").new_();
    int failures = 0;
    webcpp::asio::browser::async_wait_event(
        io.get_executor(), target, "message",
        [&](boost::system::error_code ec, const emscripten::val& event) {
            if (ec) {
                ++failures;
                return;
            }
            std::printf("event: message %d\n", event["detail"].as<int>());
        });
    send_event(target.as_handle());
    io.run();  // lint-run: main waits for the browser event
    return webcpp::test::exit_status(failures);
}

Expected output:

event: message 5

The operation removes its listener before posting completion. To receive another event, initiate another wait. Cancelling the wait does not cancel a JavaScript timer that might later dispatch an event.

Pending promise and event waits keep both the owning executor and the handler’s associated executor active. Binding a completion to another context does not require restarting that context after settlement. Cancellation transfers the completion to it; destroying the owning context releases both work guards.

Timers

steady_timer, system_timer and basic_waitable_timer are aliases of Boost.Asio’s timers on native, Emscripten and WASIp2/P3. Their executors, completion tokens, associated allocators and per-operation cancellation slots keep Boost’s interfaces and behaviour.

Use steady_timer for an interval measured by a monotonic clock, and system_timer for a deadline on the system clock. Adjusting the system clock can affect a system timer; it does not change a steady timer’s clock. A deadline makes a handler eligible to run, not a promise that the host will execute it at that exact instant.

Waiting and cancellation

On Emscripten the timers sit in Boost.Asio’s reactor queue. The run family waits through the selected suspension variant, JSPI or Asyncify (Building), allowing JavaScript to run while it waits. The reactor caps each wait at five minutes; an idle wait therefore holds one JavaScript setTimeout of at most 300 seconds. This bounds one reactor wait, not the duration a program may give a timer.

Cancelling a timer completes its pending waits with boost::asio::error::operation_aborted. An operation already ready for completion cannot be cancelled retroactively. To cancel a particular wait, bind a cancellation slot to its completion handler. A terminal signal on that slot cancels that wait without cancelling another wait on the same timer. This test cancels the other wait explicitly only after checking that it remains pending:

void a_cancellation_slot_aborts_only_its_wait() {
    std::cout << "case: a cancellation slot aborts only its wait\n";
    webcpp::asio::io_context io;
    boost::asio::cancellation_signal signal;
    const auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    webcpp::asio::steady_timer timer(io, start + 10s);
    webcpp::asio::steady_timer trigger(io, start + 10ms);
    std::size_t cancelled = 0;
    std::size_t other = 0;
    std::size_t emitted = 0;
    timer.async_wait(
        boost::asio::bind_cancellation_slot(signal.slot(), [&](boost::system::error_code ec) {
            ++cancelled;
            BOOST_TEST(ec == boost::asio::error::operation_aborted);
            BOOST_TEST_EQ(emitted, 1U);
            BOOST_TEST_EQ(other, 0U);
            // The unbound wait is still pending. Cancel it explicitly to finish the case.
            BOOST_TEST_EQ(timer.cancel(), 1U);
            std::cout << "slot cancellation: " << ec.message() << "\n";
        }));
    timer.async_wait([&](boost::system::error_code ec) {
        ++other;
        BOOST_TEST(ec == boost::asio::error::operation_aborted);
        BOOST_TEST_EQ(cancelled, 1U);
    });
    trigger.async_wait([&](boost::system::error_code ec) {
        BOOST_TEST(!ec);
        ++emitted;
        signal.emit(boost::asio::cancellation_type::terminal);
    });
    io.run();  // lint-run: the test's event loop
    BOOST_TEST_EQ(emitted, 1U);
    BOOST_TEST_EQ(cancelled, 1U);
    BOOST_TEST_EQ(other, 1U);
}

Beast’s timeouts

Boost.Beast’s basic_stream and WebSocket stream use Boost.Asio timers internally. Their timeout handling therefore uses the same reactor queue and works with both suspension variants. The test below starts a WebSocket handshake over Beast’s in-memory test stream. Its peer sends no handshake, so the completion reports boost::beast::error::timeout:

void beast_s_handshake_timeout_fires() {
    std::cout << "case: Beast's handshake timeout fires\n";
    webcpp::asio::io_context io;
    boost::beast::test::stream peer(io);
    boost::beast::websocket::stream<boost::beast::test::stream> ws(io);
    boost::beast::websocket::stream_base::timeout timeout{};
    timeout.handshake_timeout = 100ms;
    timeout.idle_timeout = boost::beast::websocket::stream_base::none();
    timeout.keep_alive_pings = false;
    ws.set_option(timeout);
    ws.next_layer().connect(peer);
    std::size_t completions = 0;
    ws.async_accept([&completions](boost::system::error_code ec) {
        ++completions;
        BOOST_TEST(ec == boost::beast::error::timeout);
        std::cout << "handshake: " << ec.message() << "\n";
    });
    io.run();  // lint-run: the test's event loop
    BOOST_TEST_EQ(completions, 1U);
}

This checks Beast’s timeout integration. It does not open a network connection or provide a browser WebSocket transport.

What the timer tests establish

Guarantee 8 records the timer contract.

The timers_native test runs natively. The timers browser tests run WebAssembly under Node with JSPI and Asyncify, each with and without exceptions. They check steady timers registered with deadlines of 60, 20 and 40 milliseconds against completion order 20, 40, 60; a system timer; whole-timer and per-operation cancellation; and Beast’s handshake timeout. The three steady deadlines share one starting instant. The tests check completion order and error values, without requiring exact elapsed times.

How to schedule deadlines and cancel a wait

Use a common clock origin when several waits belong to the same schedule. This program registers 60, 20 and 40 ms deadlines, then runs their handlers. After that run finishes, it restarts the context and cancels a separate pending wait:

#include <webcpp/asio/io_context.hpp>
#include <webcpp/asio/steady_timer.hpp>

#include <webcpp/test/exit_status.hpp>

#include <boost/asio/error.hpp>

#include <chrono>
#include <cstdio>

namespace asio = webcpp::asio;
using namespace std::chrono_literals;

int main() {
    asio::io_context io;
    const auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    asio::steady_timer sixty(io, start + 60ms);
    asio::steady_timer twenty(io, start + 20ms);
    asio::steady_timer forty(io, start + 40ms);
    const auto report = [](const char* label) {
        return [label](boost::system::error_code ec) {
            if (ec) {
                std::printf("timer error: %d\n", ec.value());
            } else {
                std::puts(label);
            }
        };
    };
    sixty.async_wait(report("60 ms"));
    twenty.async_wait(report("20 ms"));
    forty.async_wait(report("40 ms"));
    io.run();  // lint-run: main waits for the three deadlines

    io.restart();
    asio::steady_timer cancelled(io, std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point::max());
    cancelled.async_wait([](boost::system::error_code ec) {
        if (ec == boost::asio::error::operation_aborted) {
            std::puts("cancelled: operation_aborted");
        } else {
            std::printf("unexpected cancellation result: %d\n", ec.value());
        }
    });
    cancelled.cancel();
    io.run();  // lint-run: main delivers the cancelled wait's completion
    return webcpp::test::exit_status(0);
}
b2 toolset=emscripten libs/asio/example//asio_timers.output
20 ms
40 ms
60 ms
cancelled: operation_aborted

The labels identify the requested deadlines, not measured completion times. restart allows another run after the first exhausted its work. The final timer uses the clock’s maximum deadline so it remains pending until cancel. Cancelling schedules the aborted completion; the second run delivers it. Keeping these two phases separate makes the displayed order independent of when the host schedules cancellation against ready timers. For cancellation of one wait while another remains pending, use the slot example in Waiting and cancellation.

Run a Cobalt program

Boost.Cobalt’s co_main remains the application’s entry coroutine. Link /webcpp/asio//cobalt to run it with asio’s context: natively this keeps Boost.Asio’s behavior; on Emscripten it yields between bounded turns. The default turn contains at most 100 handlers, configurable with WEBCPP_ASIO_DEFAULT_MAX_HANDLERS_PER_TURN as described in Configure the build’s default turn limit. A long handler is never interrupted, and a yield offers the browser an opportunity to run rather than promising a timer deadline or a rendered frame.

The Cobalt target supports WASIp2 single-thread and WASIp3 single-thread/cooperative profiles in Target and variant capabilities. Its checked private Boost overlay removes unavailable local-socket, serial-port and process-signal dependencies from IP networking. The same thread and exception settings reach the application and compiled archive. See Build a Cobalt application for commands.

Tutorial: wait for a timer in co_main

Start with the native build setup in Building. Open libs/asio/example/asio_cobalt.cpp; this is the complete example:

#include <webcpp/test/exit_status.hpp>

#include <boost/asio/steady_timer.hpp>
#include <boost/cobalt/main.hpp>
#include <boost/cobalt/op.hpp>
#include <boost/cobalt/result.hpp>
#include <boost/cobalt/this_coro.hpp>

#include <chrono>
#include <cstdio>

boost::cobalt::main co_main([[maybe_unused]] int argc, [[maybe_unused]] char** argv) {
    // Cobalt's awaiter has static members called by the compiler's co_await expansion.
    // NOLINTNEXTLINE(readability-static-accessed-through-instance)
    const auto exec = co_await boost::cobalt::this_coro::executor;
    boost::asio::steady_timer timer(exec, std::chrono::milliseconds(50));
    auto [error] = co_await boost::cobalt::as_tuple(timer.async_wait(boost::cobalt::use_op));
    if (error) {
        std::printf("timer error: %d\n", error.value());
        co_return webcpp::test::exit_status(1);
    }
    std::puts("cobalt slept");
    co_return webcpp::test::exit_status(0);
}

this_coro::executor obtains the executor installed by the runner. The timer belongs to that executor, and co_await suspends the coroutine until its wait completes. as_tuple exposes an error as a value, so this example also builds without exception handling. It does not move a pending Cobalt task. The final exit_status call reports completion to webcpp’s example harness; an application outside that harness can simply co_return 0.

Run these commands from the superproject root:

b2 libs/asio/example//asio_cobalt.output
b2 toolset=emscripten libs/asio/example//asio_cobalt.output
b2 toolset=emscripten webcpp-suspend=asyncify libs/asio/example//asio_cobalt.output

Each run must produce the same standard output:

cobalt slept

The build compares this output against the checked-in expected file. The 50 ms is a requested timer delay, not a precise wall-clock duration. To try the result-based path, append exception-handling=off; read the upstream limitation and configuration warning below first.

How to link the integration

Add <library>/webcpp/asio//cobalt to the program’s requirements. Keep the Cobalt headers and co_main signature. The target supplies both the compiled Cobalt sources and webcpp’s replacement runner; do not also link a system Cobalt library or compile Boost’s src/main.cpp.

Exception handling follows the application. A build without exceptions prints the warning linked to Cobalt issue 287. The checked Boost 1.92 header overlay supplies the coroutine promise’s required unhandled_exception member when exceptions are disabled. It calls std::terminate if reached; it does not enable exception propagation. Compiler warnings and their warnings-as-errors policy are unchanged. Result adapters do not repair upstream operations that construct exception objects internally. This integration does not establish universal support for Cobalt without exceptions.

How to use Cobalt’s SSL stream

Include <boost/cobalt/io/ssl.hpp> and add <library>/webcpp/asio//cobalt_ssl to the program’s requirements. This optional target combines the Cobalt runner, the compiled SSL wrapper, source-built OpenSSL and embedded CAs. It supports native Clang/GCC on macOS/Linux and the WASIp2 single-thread profile with EH on/off, and the three available WASIp3 profiles in Cobalt: WASIp3. The local native validation uses macOS; it does not establish Linux runtime coverage. Browser OpenSSL and the unavailable WASIp3 cooperative/EH-on runtime are refused.

alias cobalt_ssl : : : : <library>cobalt <library>tls
  <library>/webcpp//boost_cobalt_io_ssl ;

Prepare the context with webcpp::asio::make_tls_client_context, as in How-to: configure trusted certificate authorities, and check its result. Cobalt’s SSL context is an alias for Asio’s, so the factory’s context can be passed directly to boost::cobalt::io::ssl::stream. A supplied PEM bundle replaces the embedded roots. Configure set_verify_callback with Asio’s host_name_verification for the intended hostname, and set SNI with SSL_set_tlsext_host_name on stream.native_ssl_handle(). Check both results before connecting.

native_ssl_handle() is an extension supplied by WebCPP’s checked Boost 1.92 patch. It returns a borrowed SSL* owned by the stream; do not free it or retain it after stream destruction. The inherited native_handle() still denotes the TCP socket. This extension is available only when using the patched target. Ordinary main consumers can link /webcpp//boost_cobalt_io_ssl without adding a co_main runner; the low-level target does not add WebCPP’s CA factory headers.

Reference: handshake and stream state

The wrapper supports STARTTLS: before the first handshake begins, reads and writes use plain TCP. Complete a successful handshake before sending confidential application data. secure() reports whether TLS is established, not whether the application enabled peer/hostname verification.

State or operation Behavior

Before the first handshake

secure() is false; plain TCP I/O is allowed.

Handshake succeeds

secure() becomes true before the awaiting coroutine resumes; application I/O uses TLS.

Handshake fails or is cancelled

secure() remains false; subsequent reads and writes return not_connected with zero bytes, without falling back to plaintext.

Another handshake after an attempt has started

Returns already_started; use a new stream for a new TLS attempt.

Shutdown before TLS is established

Returns no_protocol_option.

TLS shutdown completes, including with an error

secure() becomes false; further application I/O is blocked. A second shutdown returns no_protocol_option.

Both handshake overloads update the same state. The buffered overload consumes already-read handshake bytes and reports their consumed size. Keep the context, stream and buffers alive while operations are pending. Serialize state-changing operations; the wrapper does not add synchronization for overlapping handshakes, shutdown or concurrent manipulation of the underlying SSL object.

The private patch also corrects the verification callback constraint to use boost::asio::ssl::verify_context. The installed Boost tree is not modified. Rebase and verify this patch when updating Boost. The no-exceptions warning in How to link the integration still applies.

Run the local wrapper checks

From the configured superproject root, build the client and state tests:

b2 variant=release tools/openssl/test//cobalt_ssl_client tools/openssl/test//cobalt_ssl_state
b2 toolset=clang-wasip3 variant=release threading=single exception-handling=on \
  tools/openssl/test//cobalt_ssl_client tools/openssl/test//cobalt_ssl_state
b2 variant=release tools/openssl/test//cobalt_ssl_cancel
b2 toolset=clang-wasip3 variant=release tools/openssl/test//cobalt_ssl_cancel

Use each executable path printed by B2’s link action. For WASI, put Wasmtime 50.0.1 on PATH or set WASMTIME to it. The harness needs Python with TLS 1.3 and an OpenSSL CLI to generate temporary local certificates; the tested C++ program still links WebCPP’s source-built OpenSSL.

python3 tools/openssl/test/tls.py <client-path> --embedded --require-sni
python3 tools/openssl/test/tls.py <client-path> --embedded --require-sni --client-arg=buffered
python3 tools/openssl/test/tls.py <state-test-path> --state-test
python3 tools/openssl/test/tls.py <cancellation-test-path> --state-test

The client checks TLS 1.2/1.3, encrypted ping/pong, hostname, SNI, trust rejection, malformed CA data and clean shutdown. The state test checks a STARTTLS exchange, a server handshake with actual buffered ClientHello bytes, operation state read at await time, and coroutine cancellation while a handshake is pending. It uses loopback sockets and temporary certificate material, without a WASI CA preopen. The cancellation test covers pending read_some and write_some, composed io::read after receiving part of its buffer, and composed io::write under TCP backpressure. It requires operation_aborted and checks the partial byte count. The peer stops reading, socket buffers are bounded, and a zero-timeout poll confirms the TCP socket is not writable before cancellation. An SSL completion may nevertheless already be queued. If cancellation loses to successful completion, the test closes that connection and retries with a fresh one, up to eight attempts; only an actual operation_aborted satisfies the case. A watchdog catches lost cancellation; elapsed time is not the witness that an operation is pending.

For shutdown, the peer first observes close_notify but does not send its own. Closing its TCP socket produces stream_truncated; cancelling the pending shutdown produces operation_aborted. Both paths clear secure(), block further application I/O, and make a second shutdown return no_protocol_option. These checks run with TLS 1.2 and 1.3 in the supported native/WASIp2/WASIp3 profiles. Select one case with --client-arg=read_some, write_some, read, write, shutdown_error or shutdown_cancel when diagnosing a failure.

These transfer tests request terminal cancellation through the Cobalt promise. Close the socket afterward: cancellation cannot retract bytes already sent and the test does not promise safe connection reuse. Cancelling a transfer does not undo the TLS negotiation, so secure() can remain true; it is not a connection health or retry-safety indicator. Shutdown completion, including failure or cancellation, does clear that flag.

The common checked Boost 1.92 patch in tools/boost/cobalt-common connects a composition promise’s cancellation source to its completion handler. Without this connection, a cancelled composed io::read or io::write can remain pending indefinitely. The B2 target applies the fix to both compiled Cobalt operations and application-defined compositions, including consumers without SSL. The separately compiled WASIp3 acceptor object receives this patch too. cobalt_accept_cancel initiates the composed accept() overload without a client connection, cancels its Cobalt promise and requires operation_aborted with an unopened returned socket. A watchdog fails if cancellation is lost; no timer is used to guess when the accept is pending.

Why the runner changes

Cobalt’s header supplies main, which calls boost::cobalt::detail::main_promise::run_main to execute the application’s co_main. Its compiled runner owns a Boost.Asio context. webcpp replaces that definition with one using webcpp::asio::io_context, preserving the executor setup, initial post, signal cancellation and final suspension. A differently named entry coroutine would require application changes; a second co_main would conflict with the application’s definition.

The replacement reads Boost 1.92’s internal promise members: result, exec, exec_, signal_set and signal. Compiling and running the integration against the pinned Boost is its compatibility check. A future Boost change may require updating this adapter. Linking Cobalt’s original runner instead is a fallback with its original behavior, without webcpp’s turn limit; the two runners must not be linked together.

On WASIp2/P3, the runner omits the POSIX signal headers, registration and cleanup, and initializes the promise’s signal_set pointer to null. This removes its dependency on SIGINT and SIGTERM; it does not remove Asio’s internal cancellation_signal or Cobalt’s coroutine cancellation machinery. Native and Emscripten builds keep the existing process-signal integration.

A WASI host cannot request graceful shutdown through this automatic signal bridge. An application needs an explicit host/component shutdown protocol that requests cancellation on its executor and lets pending operations finish their cleanup. Calling io_context::stop() alone does not do that, and forcibly terminating the component does not guarantee C++ cleanup. No host shutdown API is supplied by this runner change.

The cobalt_main_wasip3 compile test checks the actual runner without requiring signal emulation. Public-target tests additionally execute timers, Asio socket operations through use_op, Cobalt’s own IP socket wrappers and cancellation.

Completion and limitations

The runner preserves co_return as the process exit status. Under Asyncify, a suspended main cannot simply return that status: the replacement exits explicitly after the context and signal set have been destroyed. Tests check that a timer followed by co_return 7 exits with exactly 7. With Emscripten’s default EXIT_RUNTIME=0, a debug Asyncify build may print its runtime-retained notice after std::exit; the integration does not force runtime shutdown.

The WASI runner returns the coroutine’s result to wasi-libc. In wasi-sdk 34.0, the command startup code reduces that integer to success or failure before returning through wasi:cli/run. In the local runner probe, co_return 7 therefore produces host exit status 1, while co_return 0 produces 0. This runtime mapping is separate from process-signal cancellation; do not assume that every target exposes an arbitrary nonzero exit code unchanged.

The plain Cobalt target keeps OpenSSL optional. For Cobalt’s own SSL stream, use How to use Cobalt’s SSL stream. Asio SSL streams with boost::cobalt::use_op remain available by combining /webcpp/asio//cobalt and /webcpp/asio//tls.

Reference: checks and suspension storage

cobalt_test.cpp runs 5,000 posts, checks the yield counter against the configured default (100 handlers), observes a separate page timer, and awaits both timer APIs. It does not assume that a JavaScript timer runs at a fixed callback index. The exact-exit drivers check both 7 and 0, with no completion helper in the program being checked. Run them locally with:

b2 libs/asio/test//cobalt
b2 toolset=emscripten libs/asio/test//cobalt
b2 toolset=emscripten libs/asio/test//cobalt_asyncify

The Asyncify stack probe covers the yield and forced blocking waits through both timer APIs. Its largest Cobalt observation was 1,088 bytes in a release build with the toolset’s default link, with exceptions; release linked with -O3 used at most 384 bytes. Debug used at most 1,032 bytes. The configured 8,192 bytes therefore remains unchanged. These are suspension-stack readings, not binary sizes or a guarantee about arbitrary application call depth.

Reference: release binary sizes

The timer example above was measured with Emscripten 6.0.11, Boost 1.92, C++20 and Node 26.7.0 on macOS arm64, on 2026-10-15. Each of the twelve configurations used its own build directory, with variant=release, NDEBUG, matching compile and link optimization flags, and an 8192-byte Asyncify suspension stack. Compile commands were checked for the requested optimization and exception mode; LTO objects were checked for LLVM bitcode.

All 24 page modules completed once under Node, reporting status zero and exactly cobalt slept. The -O2 modules also passed in local HeadlessChrome 153.0.8010.12 under both suspension variants and both exception modes. The other optimization profiles were not individually tested in Chrome. These are complete modules, including the Cobalt runner and the selected library code, without the Node test harness. Sizes are uncompressed bytes; JavaScript excludes the shared loader and HTML. Sockets and transports

Explanation: native sockets and browser capabilities

Native builds use Boost.Asio’s socket types directly. Emscripten builds use webcpp protocol and socket templates with the supported Boost signatures. They do not call SOCKFS or invent IP addresses through getaddrinfo. Browser TCP and UDP are unavailable unless a transport supplies the operations.

With the default transport, opening and closing an object succeeds without acquiring a network resource. Opening an already open object reports already_open. With the default transport, network operations return operation_not_supported: synchronous calls return immediately, and asynchronous calls post their completion. The error_code& overloads do not throw; throwing overloads are present only with exceptions enabled. Queries such as is_open describe the local object.

How-to: provide a transport

Specialize browser::transport<Protocol> for a protocol to provide its network operations. The specialization must be visible before first use in every translation unit using that protocol. A relay is a separate transport, not a change to an individual socket’s error policy. Its close() must cancel pending operations, release connection resources and return an error_code; the socket forwards closure and marks itself closed on success. Destruction must release resources as well. Move operations must transfer resources while preserving a usable executor in the source, so a moved-from socket can be reopened. Boost.Beast’s tcp_stream contains a Boost socket; a relay reaches Beast as an explicitly named next layer.

Reference: supported operations

Stream sockets support connect, read/write_some, send/receive, shutdown, options, endpoint queries and non-blocking settings. Datagram sockets add bind, send_to and receive_from. Acceptors support bind, listen and accept, including asynchronous acceptance into an existing or returned socket. Callbacks and deferred tokens use the same asynchronous initiation. See [asio-invariant-12] and the generated API reference for overloads.

Tutorial: observe an unsupported connection

Build and run asio_sockets on Emscripten. The object opens locally; connecting reports a value without attempting a network connection. Closing succeeds.

#include <cstdio>
#include <webcpp/asio/io_context.hpp>
#include <webcpp/asio/ip/tcp.hpp>
#include <webcpp/test/exit_status.hpp>

int main() {
    webcpp::asio::io_context io;
    webcpp::asio::ip::tcp::socket socket(io);
    boost::system::error_code ec;
    int failures = 0;
    const auto open_result = socket.open(webcpp::asio::ip::tcp::v4(), ec);
    const bool opened = !open_result && !ec && socket.is_open();
    std::printf("open: %s\n", opened ? "true" : "false");
    failures += static_cast<int>(!opened);
    const auto connect_result = socket.connect({boost::asio::ip::address_v4::loopback(), 80}, ec);
    const bool unsupported =
        connect_result == ec && ec == boost::asio::error::operation_not_supported;
    std::printf("connect: %s\n", unsupported ? "operation_not_supported" : "unexpected");
    failures += static_cast<int>(!unsupported);
    const auto close_result = socket.close(ec);
    const bool closed = !close_result && !ec && !socket.is_open();
    std::printf("close: %s\n", closed ? "ok" : "unexpected");
    failures += static_cast<int>(!closed);
    return webcpp::test::exit_status(failures);
}

Expected output:

open: true
connect: operation_not_supported
close: ok

Explanation: the resolver preserves names

On Emscripten, forward resolution constructs one entry with the original host and service, an unspecified IPv4 address and the service port. This is not a DNS lookup. A browser stream can retain the name without rewriting a client’s resolve step. A plain socket still refuses connecting to this entry.

An empty service means port 0. Decimal services accept 0 through 65535; http and ws select 80, and https and wss select 443. Named services are refused with numeric_service. Other services report service_not_found. Reverse resolution reports operation_not_supported. Async completion is posted; cancel does not retract a result already computed at initiation. See 13. Resolver entries preserve host and service.

Tutorial: retain a WebSocket service name

Build and run asio_resolver on Emscripten. The callback receives the retained name and service, port 443, and an unspecified address.

#include <cstdio>
#include <webcpp/asio/io_context.hpp>
#include <webcpp/asio/ip/tcp.hpp>
#include <webcpp/test/exit_status.hpp>

int main() {
    webcpp::asio::io_context io;
    webcpp::asio::ip::tcp::resolver resolver(io);
    int failures = 0;
    resolver.async_resolve(
        "example.com", "wss", [&](boost::system::error_code ec, const auto& results) {
            if (ec || results.size() != 1) {
                ++failures;
                return;
            }
            const auto& entry = *results.begin();
            const auto endpoint = entry.endpoint();
            std::printf("%s %s %u unspecified: %s\n", entry.host_name().c_str(),
                        entry.service_name().c_str(), static_cast<unsigned>(endpoint.port()),
                        endpoint.address().is_unspecified() ? "true" : "false");
        });
    io.run();  // lint-run: main waits for the posted resolver result
    return webcpp::test::exit_status(failures);
}

Expected output:

example.com wss 443 unspecified: true

Explanation: TLS settings

Native and WASIp2/P3 ssl names are Boost’s, with OpenSSL explicitly linked as described in TLS: build OpenSSL from source on native and WASI. In the browser, ssl::context records method, verification, options, additional roots and client-credential requests. It does not read files, parse certificates, implement TLS or execute verification callbacks. A browser stream adapter must check this record against its capabilities before use; recording a request successfully does not mean the browser honors it. The webcpp::beast browser integration consumes these settings.

A host_name_verification request owns its input string. The context copies that name into its own std::pmr::string, using the resource given to its constructor. The allocation test verifies that recorded copy separately from the request object’s standard string allocation. Other callbacks record the other kind and clear a previously recorded host.

Tutorial: configure peer verification on both targets

Build and run the tls example. Natively this configures an OpenSSL context; on Emscripten it records the same request for a browser adapter.

#include <cstdio>
#include <webcpp/asio/ssl.hpp>
#include <webcpp/test/exit_status.hpp>

int main() {
    webcpp::asio::ssl::context context(webcpp::asio::ssl::context::tlsv12_client);
    context.set_verify_mode(webcpp::asio::ssl::verify_peer);
    std::puts("context: tlsv12_client, verify_peer");
    return webcpp::test::exit_status(0);
}

Expected output on either target:

context: tlsv12_client, verify_peer

Allocation

The application supplies an allocator to the io_context through its std::allocator_arg constructor. Boost.Asio uses it for the context’s services and their I/O state. On Emscripten the bridge’s registration map uses the context’s allocator too. On Windows, a checked Boost 1.92 overlay forwards that allocator into IOCP’s internal worker and timer thread state. This includes the first timer operation, without warming up its thread or allowing an extra global allocation.

An asynchronous operation uses its completion handler’s associated allocator. Giving an allocator to the context does not associate it with all handlers: bind it to each operation with boost::asio::bind_allocator. The following compiled test binds a timer wait and ten posts, and on Emscripten the handlers posted by two bridge deliveries:

void the_user_s_allocator_takes_everything() {
    std::size_t given = 0;
    std::size_t posted = 0;
    std::size_t timed = 0;
    bool timer_succeeded = false;
#ifdef __EMSCRIPTEN__
    std::size_t received = 0;
    std::size_t promised = 0;
    std::size_t events = 0;
    std::size_t connected = 0;
    bool values_correct = true;
#endif
    {
        const allocation_window window;
        webcpp::asio::io_context io(std::allocator_arg, counted<void>(&given));
        webcpp::asio::steady_timer timer(io, std::chrono::milliseconds(5));
        timer.async_wait(
            boost::asio::bind_allocator(counted<void>(&given), [&](boost::system::error_code ec) {
                ++timed;
                timer_succeeded = !ec;
            }));
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < 10; ++i) {
            boost::asio::post(
                io, boost::asio::bind_allocator(counted<void>(&given), [&posted] { ++posted; }));
        }
#ifdef __EMSCRIPTEN__
        webcpp::asio::ip::tcp::socket socket(io);
        socket.async_connect(
            {boost::asio::ip::address_v4::loopback(), 80},
            boost::asio::bind_allocator(counted<void>(&given), [&](boost::system::error_code ec) {
                ++connected;
                values_correct =
                    values_correct && ec == boost::asio::error::operation_not_supported;
            }));
        counted_registration listener(io, &given, &received);
        auto& bridge = boost::asio::use_service<webcpp::asio::browser::bridge>(io);
        const std::uint64_t key = bridge.add(listener);
        const emscripten::val deliver = bridge.function(key);
        deliver(1);
        deliver(2);
        const auto target = emscripten::val::global("EventTarget").new_();
        webcpp::asio::browser::async_wait_event(
            io.get_executor(), target, "message",
            boost::asio::bind_allocator(counted<void>(&given),
                                        [&](boost::system::error_code ec, const emscripten::val&) {
                                            values_correct = values_correct && !ec;
                                            ++events;
                                        }));
        target.call<bool>("dispatchEvent",
                          emscripten::val::global("Event").new_(emscripten::val("message")));
        for (const bool rejected : {false, true}) {
            auto promise = emscripten::val::global("Promise").call<emscripten::val>(
                rejected ? "reject" : "resolve", 42);
            webcpp::asio::browser::async_await(
                io.get_executor(), promise,
                boost::asio::bind_allocator(
                    counted<void>(&given),
                    [&, rejected](boost::system::error_code ec, const emscripten::val& value) {
                        ++promised;
                        values_correct =
                            values_correct && value.as<int>() == 42 &&
                            (rejected ? ec == webcpp::asio::browser::error::promise_rejected : !ec);
                    }));
        }
#endif
        io.run();  // lint-run: the test's event loop
#ifdef __EMSCRIPTEN__
        bridge.remove(key);
#endif
    }
    report("supplied allocator", given);
    BOOST_TEST_EQ(posted, 10U);
    BOOST_TEST_EQ(timed, 1U);
    BOOST_TEST(timer_succeeded);
#ifdef __EMSCRIPTEN__
    BOOST_TEST_EQ(received, 2U);
    BOOST_TEST_EQ(promised, 2U);
    BOOST_TEST_EQ(events, 1U);
    BOOST_TEST_EQ(connected, 1U);
    BOOST_TEST(values_correct);
#endif
    BOOST_TEST_GT(given, 0U);
    BOOST_TEST_EQ(operator_new_calls, 0U);
    BOOST_TEST_EQ(c_allocations, 0U);
    BOOST_TEST_EQ(aligned_allocations, 0U);
}

These are runtime objects, with executors, callbacks and pointers into the current process. None of asio’s runtime objects is a relocatable object that can be shared between processes merely by placing it in shared memory.

Runtime allocations

The allocator contract does not cover these known allocations outside an operation’s associated allocator:

  • Emscripten’s select allocates its poll array with calloc on each call.

  • Asyncify allocates its unwind data when a call suspends.

  • Boost.Asio’s basic_resolver_results allocates its result entries with new. The measured operation scenario above does not resolve a name. Forward asynchronous resolution owns copies of its input names through the initiating token’s associated allocator, preserving temporary input lifetimes. Bind the allocator when creating a deferred operation; binding one only when later launching it cannot retroactively change its already-owned input storage.

  • WASI libc allocates pipe descriptors and message storage for Asio’s wakeup pipe. The test attributes only calls creating that pipe and writes to its tracked writer descriptors, removes descriptors on close, and exercises a real pipe as a positive control. Ordinary user writes and allocations remain counted.

  • OpenSSL owns context, trust-store and cryptographic allocations. Its memory hooks are process-global and must be set before any OpenSSL allocation; an Asio context cannot install a per-operation allocator for other OpenSSL users.

The allocation test replaces Emscripten’s select in the test executable with a version whose poll array is on the stack. It marks only the call to Asyncify’s allocateData while it runs, restoring the flag even if it throws, and counts those runtime allocations separately. These are test instrumentation choices, not changes to allocations in a user’s program. JavaScript heap allocations are outside these WebAssembly-memory counters.

On macOS, dyld allocates the native thread-local storage of Asio’s thread-call-stack on its first access. Before measurement the test queries running_in_this_thread on a temporary context to initialize that thread runtime. The measured context and all its operations are then constructed anew inside the window. This measures allocation routing after thread runtime initialization, not the process’s cold-start memory usage.

What the test proves

allocation_native runs natively, with allocation_native_release also checking an optimized build; allocation joins the Node-based WebAssembly tests with JSPI and Asyncify, each with and without exceptions. allocation_wasip3 checks the single-thread profile with exceptions on/off; allocation_wasip3_threads checks the supported cooperative profile without exceptions through the threads lane. A counting allocator services context construction, a timer, ten posts and on Emscripten the bridge’s two event deliveries. The measurement includes object destruction. It requires allocations through the supplied allocator and zero calls through the other counted paths, excluding only the named runtime operations above. This checks allocation routing, not a total memory limit or a proof of freedom from leaks. A separate explicit suspension verifies Asyncify’s runtime attribution: the timer may already be ready when run starts and therefore need no suspension.

The counters observe all eight global operator new forms: scalar and array, ordinary and aligned, throwing and nothrow. They also observe the C library’s malloc, calloc, realloc, aligned_alloc, posix_memalign and memalign where the platform permits it. On glibc and Emscripten the replacements forward to the underlying allocator; on macOS malloc_logger observes allocations, including aligned ones, in the C counter. Only the test’s thread and measurement windows are counted on POSIX platforms. MSVC counts global operator new calls from all threads in each window. The native allocation tests use -fno-builtin with Clang and GCC so calls to allocation functions remain observable by the hooks and are not moved across their measurement flags. This setting is confined to the test; application builds and the release size measurements keep their normal optimizations.

MSVC and AddressSanitizer builds do not count C-library allocations; they print that limitation and omit the C-specific controls. Global allocations through operator new are still counted. Local validation on one platform does not establish the behaviour of the hooks on another.

Controls deliberately call the allocation functions and post an unbound handler. Asio’s default handler storage goes through an aligned allocation, which counting only operator new would miss. A separate negative run constructs the context without its allocator and must fail. There is no allowance for an arbitrary number of extra allocations.

Promise operations allocate their state through the handler’s allocator. The allocation test covers resolution and rejection with a concrete context executor and a bound allocator, including the completion post. Explicitly erasing an executor into any_io_executor can introduce Boost-owned dispatch allocations that its handler allocator does not control; see Promises and events.

The default browser socket transport preserves an ordinary context executor’s associated allocation policy even when stored as any_io_executor. The same measurement includes an unsupported asynchronous connection with a bound allocator. Custom executors, including strands, keep their own dispatch policy.

Guarantees

These contracts apply to the supported calls described in Who may call it. The numbered anchors are stable: code and tests link to the same guarantee when its explanation moves. The reference describes individual API members; these guarantees describe their behaviour together.

  1. Natively, io_context derives from Boost.Asio’s context, shares its executor type and uses Boost’s run family. Browser scheduling options are accepted without changing native execution. The timer aliases name Boost’s types. See The names; checked by names.

  2. On Emscripten, supported handler execution happens on the stack of a run family call from main or another export configured for suspension. Posted work and events delivered through the bridge wait for such a call. See Before run, and after main; checked by reactor and bridge.

  3. A polling turn runs at most max_handlers_per_turn handlers. A full turn yields through a macrotask unless the context is stopped or its timed call has expired. A wait may run one additional handler between turns; the bound between yields is therefore at most twice the limit, not always the limit itself. Timed calls check deadlines before handlers; they cannot interrupt a running handler or guarantee when the host resumes them. See A turn at a time; checked by turn_limit, run_family and browser_render.

  4. A conforming bridge registration only posts completed work; it does not run or dispatch it inline. A listener alone is not outstanding work. See Browser events; checked by bridge.

  5. A bridge registration’s key is never reused. An event for a removed key or a destroyed context delivers nothing. The registration must outlive its key. See Browser events; checked by bridge.

  6. On Emscripten, a run family call on a context already running or delivering a bridge event reports an assertion violation and, if assertion handling permits execution to continue, returns zero without running work. It is also refused with assertions disabled. The detection scope and bypasses are listed in Who may call it; checked by detection.

  7. With exceptions enabled, a handler’s C++ exception propagates out of the run family as it does in Boost.Asio, natively and under both suspension variants. JavaScript errors have different rules. See Exceptions and JavaScript errors; checked by exceptions.

  8. Boost’s timers and Beast’s timeouts complete through the reactor on both targets. Timer cancellation retains Boost’s semantics, including cancellation of an individual wait through its associated slot. See Timers; checked by timers.

  9. Context services use the context’s allocator; operation storage uses the handler’s associated allocator. Supplying one does not implicitly supply the other. The named runtime allocations and measurement limits in Runtime allocations remain outside that routing claim. See Allocation; checked by allocation.

  10. A Promise completes its operation through the bridge with its value, or with promise_rejected and its reason. Cancellation posts operation_aborted; a later settlement cannot complete it again. See Promises and events; checked by promise and promise_cobalt.

  11. A pending Promise or event operation owns outstanding work. Destroying the context destroys its pending handler without invoking it. An event wait also removes its listener. See Promises and events; checked by promise and event.

  12. On Emscripten, network operations on a socket or acceptor fail with operation_not_supported unless a transport supplies them. Open and close manage local state; synchronous failures never block and asynchronous failures are posted. See Sockets and transports; checked by sockets and transport.

13. Resolver entries preserve host and service

On Emscripten, forward resolution returns one entry containing the original host and service, an unspecified address and the service port. A plain socket cannot connect to it. resolver_test.cpp checks service parsing and posted completion, including failures.

Testing

How to test your application

For a small program with deterministic text output, follow the compiled examples: keep an .expected file beside its source and declare the program with webcpp.example in its example Jamfile. Run the native target first, then Emscripten with JSPI and Asyncify. Compare observable completions and error values; avoid exact elapsed-time assertions, since the host can resume a ready operation later than its deadline.

Keep the context and objects captured by handlers alive until their work finishes. A cancelled operation must still complete with its cancellation error; merely requesting cancellation does not prove that it was delivered. Use Tutorial: your first asynchronous program and How to schedule deadlines and cancel a wait as executable starting points. Native and Node runs do not establish browser rendering behaviour; use a real browser when your contract depends on page events or animation.

What the library checks

asio’s tests are under test/, each declared in test/Jamfile with webcpp’s rules, for native, emscripten, wasip2 and wasip3: 266 tests in all, 85 natively, 167 on emscripten, run by node, 43 on WASIp2, and 82 on WASIp3. The WASI profiles and local commands are in Build for WASIp2 and Build and test a WASIp3 program. Each public header is also compiled alone, as the only include of its translation unit, so that a header that leans on an include it does not make fails, naming it.

<webcpp/asio/config.hpp>, which every public header of asio includes first, defines WEBCPP_ASIO_NO_EXCEPTIONS when the build has no exceptions, and a program may define it itself to turn asio’s exceptions off in a build that has them, as Boost.Asio’s BOOST_ASIO_NO_EXCEPTIONS does. The tests config, config_developer_defined and config_all_off check compiler, library-specific and global WebCPP settings.

The lanes

In addition to the WASIp2/P3 targets above, asio declares these lanes for the build and test matrix, each built from scratch with b2 -a and a --build-dir of its own. From the root of a webcpp checkout:

native

Every test and example, natively:

b2 libs/asio/test libs/asio/example
emscripten

The same on emscripten, in the default suspension variant, JSPI, each program run by node:

b2 toolset=emscripten libs/asio/test libs/asio/example
asyncify

A lane of asio’s own, on emscripten: every browser test again under Asyncify, the other suspension variant. Generate the size table separately in optimized release mode, then execute the guide examples under Asyncify:

b2 toolset=emscripten libs/asio/test//asyncify
b2 -a toolset=emscripten variant=release linkflags=-O3 libs/asio/example//asyncify
b2 toolset=emscripten webcpp-suspend=asyncify libs/asio/example
browser

A lane of asio’s own, on emscripten: the loader that picks a variant, under node, and in headless Chrome a page program that never polls, a page that keeps rendering, and the variant the loader picks:

b2 toolset=emscripten libs/asio/test/browser//browser
cobalt

An exact-exit driver runs the Cobalt entry point with statuses 7 and 0, with exceptions on and off, natively and under JSPI. A trap cannot count as the expected nonzero status:

b2 libs/asio/test//cobalt
b2 toolset=emscripten libs/asio/test//cobalt
cobalt_asyncify

The same exact-exit driver under Asyncify. It is also included in the asyncify test lane:

b2 toolset=emscripten libs/asio/test//cobalt_asyncify

b2 libs/asio/test//config builds and runs one test alone, while working on it.

Browser observations

browser_idle, browser_render and browser_loader run real page programs in headless Chrome, on both JSPI and Asyncify. The driver serves only its page, loader and build artifacts on loopback HTTP. Set CHROME to the browser executable; on macOS it otherwise finds the newest installed Playwright headless shell. Each driver has a 120-second outer bound and removes its Chrome process and temporary profile on success, failure or a termination signal.

An idle context with outstanding work must schedule exactly one positive setTimeout, at most 300 seconds, during a three-second observation. Calls to setInterval and MessagePort.postMessage are recorded too, so repeated polling cannot pass as a wait.

A self-posting handler runs for one second. The bounded run must allow at least ten animation callbacks; Boost’s unbounded control must allow none between the program’s start and completion. Callback entry times use performance.now(), not the frame timestamp supplied by requestAnimationFrame. This observes animation opportunities, not individual painted pixels or a universal frame-rate guarantee.

The yield’s MessageChannel records each complete turn at the configured limit, from resumption to the next post. The first starts at the program’s spinning line; the final partial turn is not a full-lot sample. Three historical runs at limit 1000 record callback and handler counts, turn counts, p95 and maximum turn duration in the library’s AGENTS.md. A p95 above 8 ms in either variant stops the task for the owner to decide the default. A run with no animation callbacks also stops for a decision about the witness. The maximum is reported separately. Heavy individual handlers can still block the page regardless of the handler-count limit.

The loader check runs the three-handler page normally and again after removing WebAssembly.Suspending before navigation. The page identifies the actual imported URL against the manifest before awaiting its factory, so a JSPI program whose main never returns can still report its variant. Any page exception, console.error or recorded loader error fails the run.

The test matrix

Each lane records what b2 built and ran, and webcpp’s tools/report/report.py merges the records of every lane into a matrix: a page of the libraries by lanes, and a page of each library’s tests and examples by lanes, where each cell says whether that program passed in that lane, or how it failed, at compile time, at link time or when it ran. The matrix is published with the documentation, at https://webcpporg.github.io/webcpp/report/.

How to compare release sizes and timings

Published binary sizes always use release builds. Compare the same page programs under six optimization profiles, with exceptions both enabled and disabled. Each command builds JSPI and Asyncify. Run from the superproject root, keeping the suspension-stack size and toolchain fixed:

for profile in o2 o3 os oz o3-lto oz-lto; do
    case "$profile" in
        o2) flags="-O2" ;;
        o3) flags="-O3" ;;
        os) flags="-Os" ;;
        oz) flags="-Oz" ;;
        o3-lto) flags="-O3 -flto" ;;
        oz-lto) flags="-Oz -flto" ;;
    esac
    for exceptions in on off; do
        b2 -a -j4 "--build-dir=bin/asio-size-$profile-$exceptions" \
            toolset=emscripten variant=release \
            "exception-handling=$exceptions" \
            "cxxflags=$flags" "linkflags=$flags" \
            libs/asio/example//asyncify
    done
done

variant=release supplies NDEBUG and disables debug symbols. The explicit cxxflags selects the optimization level instead of the release default -O3; the same level must be passed through linkflags for Emscripten’s final WebAssembly and JavaScript optimization. The current b2 toolset does not forward it automatically. Keep separate build directories: free-form flags do not select separate output paths in b2.

-O2 and -O3 favor execution performance; -Os and -Oz favor smaller code. -flto enables link-time optimization across translation units and must be used when compiling their object files as well as when linking. Neither a size-oriented level nor LTO guarantees a smaller result in every program.

With exception-handling=on, JSPI uses WebAssembly exceptions (-fwasm-exceptions) and Asyncify uses JavaScript-based exceptions (-fexceptions). With off, objects use -fno-exceptions, neither exception mechanism is enabled at link, and Boost’s no-exception handler is linked. The programs do not throw: this compares the cost of enabling exception support on their normal path, not throw/catch latency. Disabling exceptions changes error behavior; select it only when that contract fits the application.

Binary sizes

Each build prints its Wasm table and writes asio.sizes.md beside the variant manifests. The manifests record the Wasm byte counts; the JavaScript columns below measure the corresponding scripts themselves. These are complete page modules without the Node test harness, not asio’s isolated contribution. Add the matching Wasm and JavaScript columns for the two-file uncompressed payload. Compression, loader/HTML assets, HTTP overhead and runtime memory are outside these measurements.

The following task 14 tables cover the three examples listed below. The current command also builds the later Cobalt example; its separate measurements are in Reference: release binary sizes.

Measured on 2026-10-14 with Emscripten 6.0.11, Boost 1.92 and C++20, Node 26.7.0, macOS 27 arm64, Apple M5 Max, 128 GiB RAM. Asyncify uses an 8192-byte suspension stack. All values below are bytes. Every configuration was rebuilt in four fresh directories: one preparation build and three measured builds. File sizes were identical across the four builds. Compile and link commands were checked for optimization and exception settings; LTO object files were checked to contain LLVM bitcode. All 72 page modules matched their expected output and signalled successful completion in each runtime round. This validates these examples under Node, not the full library suite or real browsers under every profile.

Build duration

Each sample is elapsed wall time for the task 14 b2 invocation with -a -j4: compilation, linking the six page modules of the three examples above, and writing their manifests and size table. Cobalt was not registered then and is excluded from these timings; the current command builds it too. It is not a time per example or per suspension variant. One complete preparation pass populated Emscripten’s system-library cache for all profiles and exception settings. The next three passes used new output directories, alternated configuration order, and ran one b2 process at a time. The table gives the median and observed minimum to maximum, in seconds. Downloads and the preparation pass are excluded. No runtime measurements ran concurrently with compilation. These are local observations; the host was not reserved against other system activity.

Module initialization and example execution

Each sample used a fresh Node process and the exact page artifacts measured above. The runner imported the generated JavaScript and read the Wasm file before starting its clock. Initialization is measured from calling the module factory to onRuntimeInitialized; it excludes Node startup, JavaScript import/parsing, disk reads and network transfer. Execution is measured from that callback to the example’s explicit webcppTestFinished(0) signal. That signal occurs just before returning from main, before local-object cleanup. The runner waits for both the factory and the completion signal, so an Asyncify suspension cannot end a sample prematurely. It checks status zero, a single completion, exact .expected output and no stderr.

One runtime round was discarded, followed by eleven measured rounds per module, reversing configuration order between rounds. Each sample still starts a fresh process: this is not a warmed-JIT or steady-state benchmark. The tables report the median in milliseconds. Parentheses contain the 25th to 75th percentiles, calculated by linear interpolation of sorted samples. This spread describes observed variability, not a confidence interval.

The quick-start example deliberately waits 50 ms. The timers example waits until its 60 ms deadline, then tests cancellation. The turn-limit example runs 5,000 handlers with a budget of 250 per turn and yields to the event loop. Execution includes these waits, scheduling and compilation performed lazily by the runtime. None of these values is CPU-only throughput, and small differences are not evidence that a flag makes application code faster.

threads

The threads lane runs Cobalt worker/post/join, multiple Asio context runners and the WASIp3 allocator witness. The cooperative SDK profile uses exceptions off and remains distinct from simultaneous native CPU execution.

b2 -a libs/asio/test//threads
b2 -a toolset=clang-wasip3 libs/asio/test//threads
tls-integration

Real peers exercise trusted/rejected certificates, SNI, embedded/replacement roots, Cobalt TLS state, encrypted transfer cancellation, and shutdown errors and cancellation. Native single/multi profiles run with exceptions on/off; WASIp3 runs single with exceptions on/off and cooperative with exceptions off. The WASIp3 entropy control verifies that host randomness failure prevents random output and key generation. It does not measure entropy quality.

b2 -a libs/asio/test/tls//tls-integration
b2 -a toolset=clang-wasip3 libs/asio/test/tls//tls-integration

webcpp::asio::browser::main_thread_context

An execution context that posts C++ handlers onto the browser’s main runtime thread.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/asio/browser/main_thread_context.hpp>

class main_thread_context
    : public boost::asio::execution_context

Description

Construct and destroy it on the main browser thread. Its executors may be copied to workers and used with post, dispatch, defer and bind_executor. Handlers execute in ordinary browser callbacks and must not suspend WebAssembly’s stack or call an io_context run family. JavaScript values remain on their owning thread: obtain DOM values inside the main handler, and exchange ordinary C++ data with worker contexts through their executors.

Destruction discards queued handlers without invoking them. As with an Asio context, the context must outlive every call that uses its executors. The Emscripten runtime must remain alive until pending work finishes. The SDK owns proxy-queue notification storage; handler storage uses the allocator supplied to the executor. If moving or invoking a callable throws, remaining queued callables and further queued submissions are discarded. The exception propagates to the browser’s callback boundary; this context does not promise queue recovery after such a failure.

webcpp::asio::browser::async_await

Asynchronously receives a JavaScript Promise’s value or rejection reason.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/asio/browser/async_await.hpp>

template<
    class CompletionToken,
    class Executor = boost::asio::any_io_executor>
auto
async_await(
    Executor const& executor,
    emscripten::val promise,
    CompletionToken&& token);

Description

Completion is posted through the bridge, never invoked inline. Terminal, partial or total cancellation posts operation_aborted and undefined; it does not cancel the JavaScript Promise. A pending wait owns outstanding work. Destroying its context destroys its handler without calling it. Operation storage uses the handler’s associated allocator.

Return Value

The result determined by token.

Template Parameters

Name Description

Executor

The concrete or type-erased executor of the owning context.

CompletionToken

A token for void(boost::system::error_code, emscripten::val).

Parameters

Name Description

executor

The executor whose context owns the wait.

promise

A Promise or a value normalized by JavaScript Promise.resolve.

token

The completion token.

See Also

"Promises and events", in the guide.

webcpp::asio::browser::async_wait_event

Asynchronously receives the next event of type on a JavaScript EventTarget.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/asio/browser/async_wait_event.hpp>

template<
    class CompletionToken,
    class Executor = boost::asio::any_io_executor>
auto
async_wait_event(
    Executor const& executor,
    emscripten::val target,
    std::string_view type,
    CompletionToken&& token);

Description

Completion is posted through the bridge. Terminal, partial or total cancellation removes the listener and posts operation_aborted and undefined. A pending wait owns outstanding work. Context destruction removes the listener and destroys its handler silently. The event type is copied even when initiation is deferred.

Return Value

The result determined by token.

Template Parameters

Name Description

Executor

The concrete or type-erased executor of the owning context.

CompletionToken

executor

type

The event type, which need not end in a null byte.

webcpp::asio::ip::basic_resolver::async_resolve

Posts a forward result with service parsing flags.

Synopsis

template<class ResolveToken>
auto
async_resolve(
    std::string_view host,
    std::string_view service,
    flags resolve_flags,
    ResolveToken&& token);

Description

Copies the inputs with the token’s associated allocator before returning. Deferred tokens retain those copies and compute the result only when initiated. Bind an allocator to the deferred token to select its input storage allocator.

webcpp::asio::wasi::stdio_stream

A WASIp2 CLI AsyncReadStream and AsyncWriteStream driven by pollables.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/asio/wasi/stdio_stream.hpp>

class stdio_stream;

Description

Owns resource handles, without closing libc’s stdin/stdout descriptors. Only one read and one write may be outstanding at once. Operations retain buffers until completion and preserve allocator, executor and cancellation associations. Host imports may still block according to the host’s behavior.

Type Aliases

Name Description

executor_type

The executor used for readiness.

webcpp::asio::io_context

Boost.Asio’s io_context, whose run family on emscripten suspends into the browser’s event loop and yields to it after every turn of max_handlers_per_turn handlers.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/asio/io_context.hpp>

class io_context
    : public boost::asio::io_context

Description

Natively and on WASIp2/P3 it uses Boost’s run family, and its options change nothing. In a threaded browser build each context and its JavaScript bridge stay on their constructing thread. Other threads post through its executor; the run family rejects a runner on another thread. Multiple simultaneous runners of one browser context are unsupported because JavaScript values are thread-local.

webcpp::asio::make_tls_client_context

Creates a verifying TLS client context using WebCPP’s embedded Mozilla CA snapshot.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/asio/tls_client_context.hpp>

boost::system::result<ssl::context>
make_tls_client_context();

Description

No certificate files, system store, environment settings or network update are read. Updating embedded roots requires rebuilding and redeploying the program. The protocol floor, allocation and per-connection requirements are the same as the replacement overload. Link /webcpp/asio//tls to supply its dependencies.

Return Value

The context, or a tls_context_error; browser targets return unsupported_target.

See Also

"How-to: configure trusted certificate authorities", in the guide.

webcpp::asio::make_tls_client_context

Creates a verifying TLS client context trusting only the supplied authorities.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/asio/tls_client_context.hpp>

boost::system::result<ssl::context>
make_tls_client_context(std::string_view ca_pem);

Description

Native and WASIp2/P3 contexts require TLS 1.2 or newer and enable peer verification. Input consists of one or more PEM CA certificates separated only by whitespace. The certificates are copied into an independent OpenSSL store; input need not outlive this call. No system or bundled roots are added. No context is returned if any certificate is invalid. Configure hostname verification and SNI on each connection. OpenSSL owns allocations; no Asio allocator is used for its store.

Return Value

The context, or a tls_context_error; browser targets return unsupported_target.

Parameters

Name Description

ca_pem

The complete replacement PEM authority set.

See Also

"How-to: configure trusted certificate authorities", in the guide.

WEBCPP_ASIO_DEFAULT_MAX_HANDLERS_PER_TURN

The default number of ready handlers processed in one turn on Emscripten.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/asio/config.hpp>

#define WEBCPP_ASIO_DEFAULT_MAX_HANDLERS_PER_TURN

Description

Define this nonnegative integer on the compiler command line to replace 100. 0 is taken as 1 by io_context. Explicit context options override this default. Use the same definition in every translation unit, including Cobalt’s compiled runner, and rebuild when changing it. Natively it does not change scheduling. This is a handler count, not a time budget or a browser responsiveness guarantee.

See Also

"The run family", in the guide.

Defined when asio is built without exceptions: automatically when the collection has none (WEBCPP_HAS_EXCEPTIONS is not defined), or by the developer to disable them in this library alone. WEBCPP_NO_EXCEPTIONS disables them throughout the collection.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/asio/config.hpp>

#define WEBCPP_ASIO_NO_EXCEPTIONS

Description

asio raises an exception only where Boost.Asio’s own interface throws: the throwing overloads of its sockets, resolver and ssl::context (an error_code& overload stands beside each), which are absent while this is defined.

Appendix A: Changelog

Changes prepared for the first WebCPP release.

Unreleased

webcpp 0.1.0

  • Added Boost.Asio contexts and timers with browser event-loop suspension.

  • Added browser workers, main-thread handoff and turns defaulting to 100 handlers.

  • Added Promise and DOM-event operations with cancellation and allocator support.

  • Added browser socket adapters, retained resolver names and TLS settings.

  • Added WASIp2/P3 networking, UDP gather/scatter and asynchronous forward DNS.

  • Added Cobalt, CLI streams, WASI TLS and P3 cooperative-thread integration.

  • Added optional source-built OpenSSL and replaceable embedded CA certificates.

  • Fixed Cobalt TLS state/cancellation and TLS error equality across shared libraries.

  • Added capability guards and fixed configuration propagation and resolver allocation.

  • Added Diataxis guides, compiled examples and MrDocs API reference.
